monsters.name: Blue Dragon
monsters.senses: sleep and paralysis; create/destroy water at will; damage reduction 5/magic (young adult) rising to 20/magic (wyrm); spell resistance 19 (young adult) rising to 31 (great wyrm); blindsense 60 ft.; keen senses (darkvision 120 ft., low-light vision)

lore.summary: The blue is the orderly one, and no kinder for it. It rules a stretch of temperate desert as a lord rules a county — borders marked, tolls taken, trespass punished — and lairs in a vast cavern beneath the sand where it keeps its gems. It is fond of sapphires above all. Watch for a ridge of scale in a dune that was not there yesterday.

sections.title: Hunter's assessment
sections.body:
Size: Huge when grown, and the ancient ones swell far past that — a dune with a spine.
Durability: Very hard to kill. The scales stay small but thicken to the temper of shield-iron.
Defenses: A hide that hums with stored lightning and turns blades; the older ones spurn spells outright and hang false landscape over whole valleys.
Speed: It loves the hot noon air and flies well in it; on the ground it swims through loose sand as easily as it walks.
Might: Claw and bite, and a breath thrown as a long line of lightning straight down a company's rank.
Mind: Cold and methodical, vain about its own discipline. It speaks well, mimics any voice it has heard, and lies with craft.
Disposition: Lawful in the worst sense — rules, ranks and punishments, all of them its own. It holds flight from battle to be cowardice.
Bane: Lightning cannot touch it, so leave the storm-magic in the pack. It has no elemental frailty at all — but its pride forbids retreat, and a creature that will not run can be led onto ground of your choosing.

sections.title: How it fights
sections.body: It opens from above or from beneath. Buried to the eyes in sand, it waits until you are well out on open ground, then rises and lays its lightning along the length of your line. Older ones dress the desert in illusion first, so the cover you ran for was never there. It will not withdraw while it can still fight, which is the only generous thing about it.

sections.title: Margin notes
sections.body:
• Its voice is a liar. I have heard one call to me in my own captain's tones.
• Fight it on stone if you can. On sand it is already beneath you.
• Bring a gem to open with. It listens longer to those who arrive with tribute.

sections.title: Parley (wary)
sections.body: The most reasonable of the evil wyrms, which is not saying much. It keeps its word to the letter and hunts the gaps in yours. I traded a sapphire the size of my thumb for safe passage and got it — and it made me recite the terms back twice. Never mistake its order for mercy.

sections.title: Special abilities
sections.body:
Breath Weapon (Su): Using a breath weapon is a standard action; once a dragon breathes it cannot breathe again until 1d4 rounds later. A blue dragon has one type of breath weapon, a line of lightning. The line is 40 ft. long for a Small dragon, 60 ft. for Medium, 80 ft. for Large, 100 ft. for Huge and 120 ft. for Gargantuan, and is always 5 feet high and 5 feet wide. Creatures caught in the area can attempt Reflex saves to take half damage; the save DC for each age category is given in the age table.

Frightful Presence (Ex): A young adult or older dragon unsettles foes with its mere presence. The ability takes effect automatically whenever the dragon attacks, charges, or flies overhead. Creatures within a radius of 30 feet x the dragon's age category are subject to the effect if they have fewer levels than the dragon. A creature that succeeds on a Will save (DC given in the age table) is immune to that dragon's frightful presence for 24 hours. On a failure, creatures of 4 or fewer levels become panicked for 4d6 rounds and those of 5 or more levels become shaken for 4d6 rounds. Dragons ignore the frightful presence of other dragons.

Crush (Ex): A flying or jumping dragon of at least Huge size can land on opponents as a standard action, using its whole body to crush them. Crush attacks work only against opponents three or more size categories smaller than the dragon. Creatures in the affected area must succeed on a Reflex save (DC equal to that of the dragon's breath weapon) or be pinned, automatically taking bludgeoning damage during the next round unless the dragon moves off them. Damage is the listed die roll plus 1-1/2 times the dragon's Strength bonus.

Tail Sweep (Ex): A dragon of at least Gargantuan size can sweep with its tail as a standard action. The sweep affects a half-circle with a radius of 30 feet (40 feet for a Colossal dragon) extending from the edge of the dragon's space. Creatures four or more size categories smaller than the dragon are affected, taking the listed damage plus 1-1/2 times the dragon's Strength bonus; a Reflex save (DC equal to that of the dragon's breath weapon) halves the damage.

Create/Destroy Water (Sp): A blue dragon of any age can use this ability three times per day. It works like the create water spell, except that the dragon can decide to destroy water instead of creating it, which automatically spoils unattended liquids containing water. Magic items (such as potions) and items in a creature's possession must succeed on a Will save (DC equal to that of the dragon's frightful presence) or be ruined. This ability is the equivalent of a 1st-level spell.

Sound Imitation (Ex): A juvenile or older blue dragon can mimic any voice or sound it has heard, anytime it likes. Listeners must succeed on a Will save (DC equal to that of the dragon's frightful presence) to detect the ruse.

Other Spell-Like Abilities: 3/day—ventriloquism (adult or older); 1/day—hallucinatory terrain (old or older), veil (ancient or older), mirage arcana (great wyrm).

Spells: A blue dragon knows and casts arcane spells as a sorcerer of the caster level given in the age table, gaining bonus spells for its high Charisma. It can also cast cleric spells and spells from the Air, Evil, and Law domains as arcane spells.

Immunities (Ex): Immunity to electricity, sleep and paralysis effects.

Spell-Like Abilities: A dragon's spell-like abilities depend on its age and variety; it gains the abilities listed for its age plus all previous ones. Its age category or its sorcerer caster level, whichever is higher, is the caster level. The save DC is 10 + the dragon's Cha modifier + the spell level. All are usable once per day unless otherwise noted.

Damage Reduction (Su): Young adult and older dragons have damage reduction, rising from 5/magic to 20/magic with age (see the age table). Their natural weapons are treated as magic weapons for the purpose of overcoming damage reduction.

Spell Resistance (Ex): As the dragon ages it becomes more resistant to spells and spell-like abilities; the value for each age category is given in the age table.

Blindsense (Ex): The dragon can pinpoint creatures within 60 feet. Opponents it cannot actually see still have total concealment against it.

Keen Senses (Ex): A dragon sees four times as well as a human in shadowy illumination and twice as well in normal light. It also has darkvision out to 120 feet.

sections.title: Ages
sections.body: The hatchling is a small polished thing of bright azure, easily spotted against pale sand and therefore very careful. It darkens toward indigo as the desert scours it smooth; the scales gain little in breadth but a great deal in hardness, and the crackle of static about the hide sharpens until the air near it tastes of ozone. Age brings wings for the high hot air, a longer bolt of breath, the mimicry of voices, and at last the power to hang whole false countries over the dunes. Judge age by the single great horn — short and blunt in the young, long and swept back in the old — and by whether you smell the storm before you see the wyrm.

monsters.name: Green Dragon
monsters.senses: sleep and paralysis; water breathing; damage reduction 5/magic (young adult) rising to 20/magic (wyrm); spell resistance 19 (young adult) rising to 30 (great wyrm); blindsense 60 ft.; keen senses (darkvision 120 ft., low-light vision)

lore.summary: A schemer with wings. The green holds a stretch of old temperate forest, learns every path and every woodcutter in it, and would far rather own you than eat you. It picks quarrels with anything that walks, yet a promising victim it stalks for days first, listening. Where the deer have gone quiet and the leaves are bleached in patches, look up.

sections.title: Hunter's assessment
sections.body:
Size: Huge at full growth, and longer of neck than its cousins — a good deal of it is reach.
Durability: Hard to overcome; the scale broadens and lightens with the years into armour that also hides it.
Defenses: Forest-coloured plates that turn steel, and among the elders a hide that spurns spells.
Speed: Quick under the canopy, quick afoot for its bulk, and it swims and breathes water without trouble.
Might: Claw, bite, and a cone of corrosive vapour that strips leaf, cloth and lung together.
Mind: The cleverest of the chromatics and the most patient. It speaks several tongues and enjoys using them.
Disposition: It starts fights on little provocation, but its favourite weapon is a suggestion whispered to a servant it means to keep.
Bane: Acid slides off it — do not waste the flask. It has no elemental weakness at all; its flaw is an appetite of another kind. It wants to talk, to question, to know what you know, and a patient hunter can spend that curiosity.

sections.title: How it fights
sections.body: If you look weak it announces itself at once, because it enjoys the terror. If you look dangerous it follows you in silence for as long as it takes to learn your habits, then strikes where you are thinnest. It fights with vapour from the air, with claw among the trunks, and with words — bending one of your company against the rest and letting you do its killing.

sections.title: Margin notes
sections.body:
• It talks to find your weak point. Give it true words about useless things.
• Its breath sinks and lingers — never meet it in a hollow or a ditch.
• If a friend suddenly argues for the path you rejected, bind him and ask again later.

sections.title: Parley (wary)
sections.body: Of all the wyrms this one will genuinely converse. It wants news, gossip, the shape of your society, where the nearest hoard lies. I traded talk with a green for the better part of a night. Answer freely and lie carefully — every word you give it is kept, and it will use them.

sections.title: Ages
sections.body: It comes out of the shell nearly black, the scales thin and small, and it lightens as it grows: forest, then emerald, then a pale olive that disappears against summer leaves. Length arrives before bulk, the neck running out long while the crest of horns above the eyes rises and spreads. The breath widens from a puff to a rolling cone of corrosive gas, and the mind sharpens all the while — first a whispered suggestion, then outright mastery of a man's will, then command over the wood itself. Judge age by colour and crest: the darker and blunter, the younger. If the trees themselves seem to shift to its liking, leave.

monsters.name: White Dragon
monsters.senses: sleep and paralysis; vulnerability to fire; icewalking; damage reduction 5/magic (young adult) rising to 20/magic (wyrm); spell resistance 16 (young adult) rising to 27 (great wyrm); blindsense 60 ft.; keen senses (darkvision 120 ft., low-light vision)

lore.summary: The least of the chromatics and the most nakedly a beast. The white haunts cold mountains and the ice beneath them, tunnels through drift, swims frigid water, and nurses grudges long after it has forgotten what caused them. It hoards as all its kin do, but chiefly it is hungry. Where a glacier is scored by a slot too smooth for weather, that is the door.

sections.title: Hunter's assessment
sections.body:
Size: Large in its prime — smaller than its cousins, and it makes the difference up in temper.
Durability: Tough as a walrus and twice as stubborn, under mirror-bright scales that dull and grey with age.
Defenses: Thick hide that blades labour against, and the elder ones begin to turn magic aside.
Speed: The most mobile of the chromatics: it runs, burrows through snow and ice, swims well, walks sheer ice as though it were a floor, and flies.
Might: Claw, bite, and a cone of killing cold; the older ones raise walls of ice and freezing fogs to pen you where they want you.
Mind: Dull. It has the dragon tongue and a few words of yours, but it thinks in terms of prey, cold and grudges.
Disposition: Feral and ambush-minded. It strikes first and considers afterwards, if at all.
Bane: Cold is nothing to it — save your frost. Fire hurts it badly, and it is dim enough to be baited and slow enough to be outthought.

sections.title: How it fights
sections.body: It comes down out of a white sky, or up through the snow and water you were standing on, breathes its cone across the lot of you, then falls on whichever one is still upright and finishes that one alone. It chooses ice to fight on, where you slip and it does not, and if the day turns against it, it goes into the drift and returns from another quarter.

sections.title: Margin notes
sections.body:
• Bring fire. Any fire. It is the only mercy this one offers.
• Never fight it standing on ice — it walks that surface as you walk a floor.
• It hides in the snow you are crossing. Prod the drifts ahead with a spear.

sections.title: Parley (never)
sections.body: It has the dragon tongue and a few words of ours, and neither will save you. I tried twice. The first listened to three sentences and then ate the horse I was standing beside. Talk needs vanity or greed to work upon; this one has only hunger. Strike first, and strike warm.

sections.title: Threat
sections.body: Grave — A grave peril

sections.title: Stat block (SRD)
sections.body:

sections.title: Special abilities
sections.body:
Breath Weapon (Su): Using a breath weapon is a standard action; once a dragon breathes it cannot breathe again until 1d4 rounds later. A white dragon has one type of breath weapon, a cone of cold. The cone is 15 ft. long for a Tiny dragon, 20 ft. for Small, 30 ft. for Medium, 40 ft. for Large, 50 ft. for Huge and 60 ft. for Gargantuan. Creatures caught in the area can attempt Reflex saves to take half damage; the save DC for each age category is given in the age table.

Frightful Presence (Ex): A young adult or older dragon unsettles foes with its mere presence. The ability takes effect automatically whenever the dragon attacks, charges, or flies overhead. Creatures within a radius of 30 feet x the dragon's age category are subject to the effect if they have fewer levels than the dragon. A creature that succeeds on a Will save (DC given in the age table) is immune to that dragon's frightful presence for 24 hours. On a failure, creatures of 4 or fewer levels become panicked for 4d6 rounds and those of 5 or more levels become shaken for 4d6 rounds. Dragons ignore the frightful presence of other dragons.

Crush (Ex): A flying or jumping dragon of at least Huge size can land on opponents as a standard action, using its whole body to crush them. Crush attacks work only against opponents three or more size categories smaller than the dragon. Creatures in the affected area must succeed on a Reflex save (DC equal to that of the dragon's breath weapon) or be pinned, automatically taking bludgeoning damage during the next round unless the dragon moves off them. Damage is the listed die roll plus 1-1/2 times the dragon's Strength bonus.

Tail Sweep (Ex): A dragon of at least Gargantuan size can sweep with its tail as a standard action. The sweep affects a half-circle with a radius of 30 feet (40 feet for a Colossal dragon) extending from the edge of the dragon's space. Creatures four or more size categories smaller than the dragon are affected, taking the listed damage plus 1-1/2 times the dragon's Strength bonus; a Reflex save (DC equal to that of the dragon's breath weapon) halves the damage.

Icewalking (Ex): This ability works like the spider climb spell, but the surfaces the dragon climbs must be icy. It is always in effect.

Freezing Fog (Sp): An old or older white dragon can use this ability three times per day. It is similar to a solid fog spell but also causes a rime of slippery ice to form on any surface the fog touches, creating the effect of a grease spell. The dragon is immune to the grease effect because of its icewalking ability. This ability is the equivalent of a 5th-level spell.

Other Spell-Like Abilities: 3/day—fog cloud (juvenile or older), gust of wind (adult or older), wall of ice (ancient or older); 1/day—control weather (great wyrm).

Spells: An adult or older white dragon knows and casts arcane spells as a sorcerer of the caster level given in the age table, gaining bonus spells for its Charisma.

Immunities (Ex): Immunity to cold, sleep and paralysis effects. A white dragon has vulnerability to fire.

Spell-Like Abilities: A dragon's spell-like abilities depend on its age and variety; it gains the abilities listed for its age plus all previous ones. Its age category or its sorcerer caster level, whichever is higher, is the caster level. The save DC is 10 + the dragon's Cha modifier + the spell level. All are usable once per day unless otherwise noted.

Damage Reduction (Su): Young adult and older dragons have damage reduction, rising from 5/magic to 20/magic with age (see the age table). Their natural weapons are treated as magic weapons for the purpose of overcoming damage reduction.

Spell Resistance (Ex): As the dragon ages it becomes more resistant to spells and spell-like abilities; the value for each age category is given in the age table.

Blindsense (Ex): The dragon can pinpoint creatures within 60 feet. Opponents it cannot actually see still have total concealment against it.

Keen Senses (Ex): A dragon sees four times as well as a human in shadowy illumination and twice as well in normal light. It also has darkvision out to 120 feet.

sections.title: Ages
sections.body: It hatches with scales like small mirrors and stays bright through its early years; the sheen dies away with growth, and by the old ages pale blue and grey are mixed through the white. Size comes slowly and stays modest by dragon reckoning, but the cold of the breath deepens all the while, and its trick with weather grows from a puff of fog to freezing mist, walls of ice, and finally the temper of the sky itself. It never becomes clever. Judge age by the shine: a mirror-bright hide is a young thing, dangerous but manageable; a dull grey-white one has been killing on that mountain since your grandfather's day.

lore.summary: Raiders out of the cold mountains, and proud of it. Frost giants live in tribes under a jarl, in ice caves and rough stone halls, keeping winter wolves as hounds and ogres as servants, and they come down on the low country whenever the passes allow. They dress in pelts and horned helms, and they hold a stolen thing more honourable than a bought one.

sections.title: Hunter's assessment
sections.body:
Size: Large — more than twice a tall man's height, and heavier than a warhorse.
Durability: Very hard to put down. They take wounds that would end a bear and keep swinging.
Defenses: Hide like frozen leather, mail shirts over it, horned helms above; blizzard and frostbite mean nothing to them at all.
Speed: A long ground-eating stride, and sure-footed on snow and ice where you are not.
Might: Huge axes swung two-handed, blows that carry clean through one man and into the next, and hurled stones that arrive like siege shot.
Mind: Ordinary wit and better tactics than you expect — ambush, high ground, and a keen sense of whom to kill first.
Disposition: Cruel raiders who respect strength above all and settle much among themselves by open challenge.
Bane: Cold cannot harm them in the least. Fire can, and badly — a torch is worth more here than a good sword. And they pluck thrown stones out of the air, so do not throw stones.

sections.title: How it fights
sections.body: They open at a distance, pitching rocks until the stones run out or you close, then wade in with axes that cleave through a man and keep going. Their favourite trick is to lie buried in the snow at the crest of an icy slope and let you spend yourself climbing to them. A raiding band brings winter wolves and ogres; a whole tribe may keep a young white wyrm on a chain of tribute.

sections.title: Margin notes
sections.body:
• Fire. Torches, oil, a burning brand — they hate it, and it is light to carry.
• Do not throw rocks at them. They catch them. I have watched it happen twice.
• Take the high ground first or do not take the fight. They are already up there.

sections.title: Parley (wary)
sections.body: They will talk, and they will hold to what they said, provided you have shown them something worth respecting. I once stood a challenge with a jarl's son over a frozen river and lost honestly; they fed me, argued about me all night, and let me walk out at dawn. Show fear and none of that happens.

sections.title: Threat
sections.body: Grave — A grave peril

sections.title: Special abilities
sections.body:
Rock Throwing (Ex): Adult giants are accomplished rock throwers and gain a +1 racial bonus on attack rolls when throwing rocks. A giant of at least Large size can hurl rocks weighing 40 to 50 pounds each (Small objects) up to five range increments. The range increment is 120 feet for a frost giant’s thrown rocks.

Rock Catching (Ex): A giant of at least Large size can catch Small, Medium or Large rocks (or projectiles of similar shape). Once per round a giant that would normally be hit by a rock can make a Reflex save to catch it as a free action. The DC is 15 for a Small rock, 20 for a Medium one and 25 for a Large one; if the projectile provides a magical bonus on attack rolls, the DC increases by that amount. The giant must be aware of the attack in order to attempt a catch.

Immunity to Cold and Vulnerability to Fire (Ex): A frost giant takes no damage from cold. It takes half again as much (+50%) damage as normal from fire, regardless of whether a saving throw is allowed or whether the save succeeds or fails.

Tactics: Frost giants usually start combat at a distance, throwing rocks until they run out of ammunition or the opponent closes, then wading in with their enormous battleaxes. A favourite tactic is to lay an ambush by hiding buried in the snow at the top of an icy or snowy slope, where opponents will have difficulty reaching them.

monsters.name: Silver Dragon
monsters.senses: and paralysis; vulnerability to fire; blindsense 60 ft.; darkvision 120 ft.; low-light vision; keen senses; damage reduction and spell resistance increasing with age

lore.summary: Silver dragons keep the cloud tops and the high cold peaks, treading fog as a man treads a floor. Of all wyrms they are likeliest to walk among us — an old shepherd, a grey-eyed knight, a hound asleep by an inn fire — watching how we use the weak. Meet one honestly and you may never learn you met it at all.

sections.title: Hunter's assessment
sections.body:
Size: Huge — a mountain of bright, seamless scale, wyrmling blue-grey brightening to mirror-silver with the years.
Durability: Vast. It will outlast a whole company and be barely winded.
Defenses: Scales like fitted plate that turn steel; sorcery slides off it; frost and killing chill mean nothing to it, and no charm of sleep or stiffening will hold it.
Speed: Slow and stately afoot, terrible on the wing, and it walks upon cloud and fog as if on flagstone.
Might: Claw, bite and buffeting wing that break bone through mail; a cone of searing cold, and a second breath of pale gas that locks a man rigid where he stands.
Mind: Keen as any sage, lawful and good, and fluent in more tongues than you have seen kingdoms.
Disposition: Not violent. It shuns a fight unless faced with the cruel or the aggressive — and then it is patient, thorough and merciless in judgement.
Bane: Cold is wasted breath against it — bring flame or nothing. Its true seam is its mercy: it will spare a foe who yields, and a liar can buy his life with the same lie twice.

sections.title: How it fights
sections.body: It fights from above and from cover. It draws fog about itself, or calls weather to make cloud on a clear day, then hangs in it unseen until it can fall on you from a blind angle. Against a company on the ground it blinds and scatters them with mist, then breathes cold; against fliers it snatches and lets go. The oldest of them tip the sky itself on end and pluck the falling out of the air. It gives warning first. It gives warning only once.

sections.title: Margin notes
sections.body:
• The white-haired stranger who joins your fire on a mountain road may be your quarry. Mind your mouth.
• Frost, ice, winter magic — all useless. Carry fire and steel, or carry an apology.
• The pale breath, not the cold one, is the killer. Locked stiff before a wyrm is how good hunters end.

sections.title: Parley (open)
sections.body: Speak first, always. I have shared bread with three, and only learned what one was when it thanked me and stepped off the cliff edge into the air. But understand: it is weighing you while you talk. Answer plainly, admit your errands, and do not flatter. It has heard better lies than yours from better men.

sections.title: Ages
sections.body: A silver hatches blue-grey with silver lights along the scale, no bigger than a hound, and already able to breathe frost. As it grows the grey burns away and the scales knit until the eye cannot find the seams between them; by adulthood it shines like a poured mirror, and in the great wyrm the pupils are gone and the eyes are two blank moons. With size comes craft: first the cloud-walking and the falling-feather trick, then fog at will, then command of wind, then weather, and at the last the power to turn falling upside down. Judge it by the scales and the eyes — mottled and dull with a visible pupil is young; smooth as a coin's face with molten, pupilless eyes is a wyrm older than the road you came by. Judge it also by its patience. A young one argues. An old one waits.

monsters.senses: and paralysis; vulnerability to cold; blindsense 60 ft.; darkvision 120 ft.; low-light vision; keen senses; damage reduction and spell resistance increasing with age

lore.summary: The noblest of the wyrms, and it knows it. Gold dragons keep warm open country and quiet shrines, whiskered and grave-faced, their eyes fading to pools of molten metal as the centuries pass. They walk among men as pilgrims, judges and beggars, and they will parley before they will ever burn. Being judged by one is worse than being fought by one.

sections.title: Hunter's assessment
sections.body:
Size: Huge — golden from crown to tail-tip, bewhiskered like an old scholar, and heavier than the hall it sits in.
Durability: Immense. Of all wyrms, the hardest thing in the world to kill.
Defenses: Scales that shrug off honest steel, strong resistance to sorcery, utter indifference to fire, and no sleep-charm or stiffening will take it. It also breathes water as easily as air.
Speed: Ponderous on the ground, swift and sure aloft, and equally at home beneath the waves.
Might: Claw and bite and tail that shatter shield-walls; a cone of fire, and a second breath of grey gas that leaves a strong man unable to lift his own sword.
Mind: The wisest thing you will ever meet. Lawful, good, learned, and a spellcaster to rival any archmage — it reads your motive before you finish the sentence.
Disposition: It talks first. It will hear your case, name your fault, and offer you a chance to mend it. Refuse, and it stops talking.
Bane: Fire is nothing to it — a torch-bearer only amuses it. Its weakness is its own courtesy: it parleys when it ought to strike, and it will hold to a bargain struck with a wicked man because it gave its word.

sections.title: How it fights
sections.body: It parleys first, and while it parleys it is reading you — your motive, your nerve, your lie. When words fail it fights as a mage first and a wyrm second: it blesses itself and its allies, wraps itself in wards and shields of flame, and answers a formed company with killing cloud and stunning fire from a distance. Those who close with it are mazed away or crushed. The elder ones carry a lucky stone in the hide that turns aside the very strokes that ought to fell them, and they seem to know an hour beforehand that you were coming.

sections.title: Margin notes
sections.body:
• Never lie to a gold. It is not that it catches you. It is that it lets you finish.
• Fire is worthless here. Cold steel, cold magic, and better footing than it has.
• Bargain honestly and it will keep the bargain to the letter. So mind the letter.

sections.title: Parley (open)
sections.body: It will always give you words. Take them — but know you are being weighed, and it is better at the weighing than you are at the answering. I once spent a whole night justifying a killing to a gold in the shape of a lame old priest. It let me go at dawn. I still am not certain it agreed.

Luck Bonus (Sp): Once per day an adult or older gold dragon can touch a gem, usually one embedded in its own hide, and enspell it to bring good luck. While the dragon carries the gem, it and every good creature within a 10-foot radius per age category gains a +1 luck bonus on all saving throws and similar rolls, as a stone of good luck. If the dragon gives the gem away, only the bearer gains the bonus. The effect lasts 1d3 hours plus 3 hours per age category and ends if the gem is destroyed. This ability is the equivalent of a 2nd-level spell.

Detect Gems (Sp): An old or older gold dragon can use this ability three times per day. It is a divination effect like detect magic, except that it finds only gems. The dragon scans a 60-degree arc: one round of concentration reveals whether gems lie in the arc, two rounds the exact number, and three rounds their exact location, type, and value. This ability is the equivalent of a 2nd-level spell.

Spells: A gold dragon casts spells as a sorcerer, beginning at caster level 1st as a young dragon and reaching caster level 19th as a great wyrm. It can also cast cleric spells and spells from the Law, Luck, and Good domains as arcane spells.

sections.title: Ages
sections.body: It hatches dark yellow, flecked with metal as though someone had spilled coin-shavings across it; the flecks widen year on year until, at its adult prime, no dull scale is left and the whole beast is one poured ingot. The face gains its whiskers and its sagging, sagacious look; the pupils bleach away until the eyes are two pools of molten gold. The craft grows with the hide: blessings first, then the trick of the lucky gem, then the sense that finds every jewel within a hillside, then the power to lay a binding errand on a man, then a bursting light like a small sun, and at the last a foresight that no ambush can defeat. Read it in the flecks and the eyes. Speckled scale and a visible pupil, and you face a youngster. A seamless golden hull and blind molten eyes, and you face something that was old when your grandsire's kingdom was founded.

lore.summary: Copper dragons haunt dry rocky hills and stony gorges, ruddy-brown at hatching and warm burnished copper by their prime. They are thieves, jesters and riddlers, and they would sooner make a fool of you than a corpse. Every meeting with one is a test you did not know you had entered, and the fee for failing it is usually your dignity — usually.

sections.title: Hunter's assessment
sections.body:
Size: Large — long, lean and gorge-shaped, with backswept horns and eyes that fade to glowing turquoise in the ancient ones.
Durability: Formidable. It can absorb more punishment than any warband you can raise.
Defenses: Coppery plate that turns most weapons, a strong resistance to spellcraft, complete immunity to acid, and no charm of sleep or stiffening holds it.
Speed: Quick aloft and quicker in broken country — it runs up a sheer rock face as easily as you cross a room, which is how it always has the high ground.
Might: Claw, bite and tail-lash; a scouring line of acid, and a second breath of gas that leaves a man wading through his own movements.
Mind: Sharp, chaotic and good-hearted, with a magpie's love of treasure and a jester's love of an audience. It knows the stones under you better than you do.
Disposition: It taunts. It baits. It wants you angry, foolish and off balance, and it will let you live if you make it laugh.
Bane: Acid is wasted upon it, and it will out-climb you on any rock in the world. But its vanity is a door: it cannot let a jest go unanswered, and while it is being clever it is not being careful. Draw it onto open flat ground where there is no stone to soften and no wall to fly you into.

sections.title: How it fights
sections.body: It does not open with violence; it opens with mockery, and the mockery is a tactic. When it does commit, it turns the ground itself against you — good hard rock goes to sucking mud underfoot, and while you are mired it pushes you deeper or plucks you out and carries you up to drop you. Against fliers it retreats into narrow stony gorges, runs the walls like a lizard, and works you into colliding with the rock. Older ones raise stone walls to split a party and rearrange the whole hillside at need.

sections.title: Margin notes
sections.body:
• Come with a riddle. A new one. It has heard all the old ones and it will tell you so.
• It will out-climb you on any rock ever quarried. Fight it on the flat or not at all.
• Acid does nothing. And do not stand still on stone — the ground is its weapon before its breath is.

sections.title: Parley (open)
sections.body: Words work, but you must earn them. It wants a riddle it has not heard or a jest it has not told, and it will not harm a creature that gives it one. I bought passage through the Ochre Scarps with a filthy dockside rhyme. Laugh at its own jokes, too — sulking at a copper is how the trouble starts.

sections.title: Ages
sections.body: A copper hatchling is a dull ruddy brown with only a metal hint to it. The scales fine down and warm as it grows, taking a soft gloss by young adulthood; in the very old a green tint creeps in, and the pupils fade until a great wyrm's eyes are lamps of turquoise. Its craft follows the stone: first only its climbing and its wit, then the shaping of rock in its claws, then the trick of turning rock to mud and mud to rock, then walls raised out of bare ground, and at the last the moving of whole hills. Judge it by the gloss and the eyes — dull brown with a black pupil is a youngster whose jokes are bad; green-tinged copper with turquoise lamps for eyes is a wyrm whose jokes are old, well-practised and lethal.

lore.summary: Brass dragons keep the deep deserts, mottled brown at hatching and burnished to a warm sheen with age, with smooth head-plates and bladed chin horns. They are the most talkative creatures under the sun and the loneliest, and they collect gossip the way other wyrms collect coin. The danger of a brass is not that it will eat you. It is that it will not let you leave.

sections.title: Hunter's assessment
sections.body:
Size: Large — brassy and warm-hued, with grand smooth head-plates, bladed chin horns, and green-mottled wings that darken with the years.
Durability: Great. Least of the metallics, and still far beyond any mortal fighter.
Defenses: Burnished scale that blunts weapons, solid resistance to magic, complete immunity to fire and to heat of any kind, and neither sleep nor stiffening charms touch it.
Speed: Strong on the wing, and able to sink into loose sand and vanish as though it had never been.
Might: Claw, bite and chin horns; a searing line of fire, and a second breath of sleep gas that drops the strongest man where he stands, however hardened he is.
Mind: Bright, curious, chaotic and good, endlessly well informed — it speaks with the beasts of the waste at will and hears everything that crosses the sand.
Disposition: It wants conversation, not blood. Try to walk away without giving it any and it will take offence and make you stay.
Bane: Fire and heat will never touch it. But it is the least of the metallics and the least warlike, and its own tongue undoes it: keep it talking and it will forget to attack. Young ones simply flee and bury themselves rather than fight.

sections.title: How it fights
sections.body: It would far rather talk, and its first resort against someone rude enough to leave is not the flame but the persuasion — a suggestion planted in the ear, or a dose of sleep gas. Men who take that breath wake pinned, or buried to the neck in sand, with a dragon settled comfortably nearby waiting to resume the conversation. Pushed to real danger, a young one flies out of sight and burrows into the dune to hide; an older one scorns that, calls the wind and the weather to its own advantage, and only then uses the fire.

sections.title: Margin notes
sections.body:
• Do not walk off mid-sentence. That is what the sleep gas is for, and you will wake buried to the chin.
• Fire is useless. Bring cold, and bring patience.
• Best source of news in any waste. Ask it what has passed this way — it will know, and it will tell you at length.

sections.title: Parley (open)
sections.body: The easiest parley in the world to begin and the hardest to end. It wants news, gossip, anything from beyond the sand. Give it freely and it will guide you, water you, warn you of what lies ahead. Only never try to slip away quietly. I lost most of a week to one that simply would not stop, and I have never been made so welcome anywhere.

sections.title: Ages
sections.body: It comes out of the shell a dull mottled brown with barely a shine to it. Year on year the scales brighten to true brass and take a burnished warmth; the head-plates broaden and smooth, the chin horns lengthen and sharpen, the green at the wing edges darkens, and the pupils fade until the eyes are orbs of molten metal. Its gifts grow with its talk: it speaks to beasts from the first, then learns to ward its companions against the killing heat and cold of the waste, then to plant a suggestion in a mind, then to summon the winds, then the weather itself, and the greatest of them can call a spirit of the air out of the empty sky. Read it by the sheen and the horns — mottled and dull with stubby chin blades is a youngster who will bolt; deep burnished brass with long bright horns and molten eyes is a wyrm that has been holding this stretch of desert for a very long time.

lore.summary: Coal-skinned, flame-haired and built like a forge-anvil, fire giants hold the halls beneath volcanoes and the hot valleys where the ground still smokes. They are disciplined, cruel and superb smiths, drilled in ordered ranks under a king, and they take slaves to work the bellows. Where you find blackened plate and a hammer-ring underground, you have found their gate.

sections.title: Hunter's assessment
sections.body:
Size: Large — twice the height of a tall man and heavier than a cart-horse team, with hair like burning orange straw.
Durability: Very tough. Expect to be at it a long while, and to be hit hard throughout.
Defenses: Half-plate of blackened steel over hide like cooked leather, and utter immunity to fire — lava, forge-heat and flame-magic all pass over it harmless.
Speed: Not fast, and armour makes it slower still. You can outrun one on open ground; you cannot outrun what it throws.
Might: Prodigious. It favours a great flaming blade, and one stroke will end an armoured man. It hurls boulders heated in the lava, which strike burning.
Mind: Clever for a giant and far more disciplined than its kin — lawful, evil, organised, and it fights in formation under officers and priests.
Disposition: Warlike and cruel. It takes thralls for the forges and reckons your worth in labour, not in ransom.
Bane: Cold. Frost and ice bite it far worse than they would bite you, and a winter's blast will break one faster than any blade. Fire it drinks like ale, so leave your flaming sword in its sheath. Beware also its habit of seizing smaller foes and pitching them into the nearest lava.

sections.title: How it fights
sections.body: It fights in ordered ranks, not as a mob, and its priests fight beside it. At a distance it heats stones in a lava pool, geyser or forge-fire and throws them, so that the impact burns as well as breaks. In reach it prefers a great flaming sword and swings to end the fight in a stroke or two. Given the chance it will grab a smaller foe outright and throw them somewhere very hot — a vent, a crucible, a lava channel — which kills as surely as the blade and costs it nothing.

sections.title: Margin notes
sections.body:
• Cold. Everything cold. Frost-brand, ice, a winter blast — nothing else fells one so quickly.
• Do not let it lay hands on you. It does not stab you; it throws you into the lava.
• Their rocks come out of the fire. If your shield is scorched, look up — the next one is already coming.

sections.title: Parley (wary)
sections.body: Words are possible, barely. They respect strength, rank and craft, and they honour a bargain while the bargain profits them. I traded a dwarf-forged blade for safe passage through the Cinder Deep and was watched by four of them the whole way out. Never parley without an exit at your back, and never in their hall.

sections.title: Special abilities
sections.body:

A giant of at least Large size can hurl rocks weighing 40 to 50 pounds each (Small objects) up to five range increments. The range increment is 120 feet for a fire giant’s thrown rocks.

Heated Rocks (Ex): Fire giants heat their rocks in a nearby fire, geyser or lava pool, so that a thrown rock deals an extra 2d6 points of fire damage on a hit.

Rock Catching (Ex): A giant of at least Large size can catch Small, Medium or Large rocks (or projectiles of similar shape). Once per round a giant that would normally be hit by a rock can make a Reflex save to catch it as a free action. The DC is 15 for a Small rock, 20 for a Medium one and 25 for a Large one; if the projectile provides a magical bonus on attack rolls, the DC increases by that amount. The giant must be aware of the attack in order to attempt a catch.

Immunity to Fire and Vulnerability to Cold (Ex): A fire giant takes no damage from fire. It takes half again as much (+50%) damage as normal from cold, regardless of whether a saving throw is allowed or whether the save succeeds or fails.

Tactics: Fire giants favour magic flaming swords in melee when they can get them, and are fond of grabbing smaller opponents and tossing them somewhere very hot.

lore.summary: Gaunt grey giants of the high mountain caves, dwelling apart from the world and content to be forgotten by it. They wear thick leathers dyed the browns and greys of the scree, and will stand motionless against a cliff face until the rock itself seems to step forward. Carvers, herders and hurlers of stone, met on the shoulders of the peaks — shy, not cruel.

sections.title: Hunter's assessment
sections.body:
Size: Large — a lean, long-limbed giant, half again the height of the tallest man you know.
Durability: Mountain-bred and enduring; it will still be standing long after you want it to be.
Defenses: Stone-grey hide like weathered granite under heavy hide armour, and it can pluck a thrown rock out of the air and keep it.
Speed: A long stride on open scree, a fine climber, and it leaps gaps that would stop a horse.
Might: Tremendous — a club chiselled from living rock, and boulders thrown farther and truer than you would credit.
Mind: As shrewd as a thoughtful man, patient, and very long-lived; the elders among them command an old earth-magic that shapes and questions the stone itself.
Disposition: Neutral by temper and reclusive by choice — wary of strangers, quick to withdraw, and cruel only when cornered or robbed.
Bane: It would rather not fight you at all, and that is the seam. It has no venom, no breath, no sorcery in the common run of them — only distance and a club. Close under its reach and stay closed, and half its craft is gone. Fight it in the open scree at range and it will hit you from a hill you cannot even see.

sections.title: How it fights
sections.body: It fights at distance for as long as you allow it. A favoured trick is to stand utterly still against a rock wall until you have walked past, then step out and open with a thrown boulder — the first stone almost always arrives as a surprise. Thereafter it keeps its ground high and its stones flying, catching what you throw back and returning it. Only when it cannot avoid the press does it take up the stone club, and then it strikes fast at anything that steps within its long reach.

sections.title: Margin notes
sections.body:
• That grey boulder beside the path has knees. Look twice before you pass it.
• Get inside its arm and stay there. At a stone's throw you are simply a target it has already ranged.
• Ask after the elder before you draw. Half the quarrels I have seen with these folk were a misunderstanding about a goat.

sections.title: Parley (open)
sections.body: Words work here more often than steel. I have shared a fire with a hunting party of them and traded salt for a carved bowl I still own. Come up the slope openly, empty-handed, and speak in the giants' tongue if you have it. Do not haggle hard, and never touch their carvings.

Stone Giant Elders: Some stone giants develop special abilities related to their environment. These elders have Charisma scores of at least 15 and spell-like abilities, which they use as 10th-level sorcerers. Spell-Like Abilities: 1/day—stone shape, stone tell, and either transmute rock to mud or transmute mud to rock (DC 17). Caster level 10th; the save DC is Charisma-based. One in ten elders is a sorcerer, usually of 3rd to 6th level. An elder is Challenge Rating 9 with level adjustment +6; its other statistics match those of a common stone giant.

Tactics: Stone giants fight from a distance whenever possible, but if they cannot avoid melee they use gigantic clubs chiselled out of stone. A favourite tactic is to stand nearly motionless, blending in with the background, then move forward to throw rocks and surprise their foes.

lore.summary: Lords of the thunder-line, silver-haired and sky-eyed, keeping castles upon the high peaks and upon cloudbanks that have no business bearing a hall at all. They dress to declare their station and are fond of the harp. Some are generous hosts who will feed a lost traveller; as many reckon the lowlands their larder. Both will judge you the moment you arrive.

sections.title: Hunter's assessment
sections.body:
Size: Huge — a head and shoulders above the mountain giants, and heavier than a wagon and its team.
Durability: Prodigious. Whatever you do to it, expect to do it for a long while.
Defenses: Thick hide beneath fine mail, and it catches thrown rocks from the air as easily as a man catches an apple.
Speed: An unhurried stride that eats ground faster than you can run, and it can lift itself and a great weight straight up into the air at will.
Might: Titanic — a two-handed morningstar built for something larger still, and blows that hurl a mailed man clean off the parapet.
Mind: Clever, cultured and musical, and it plans a fight the way a captain does. It will smell you long before it sees you.
Disposition: Proud and aristocratic to the bone. Rank, dress and manner are everything; some are decent and generous, others coldly wicked, and nothing in the face tells you which.
Bane: There is no soft place in the hide worth naming — the seam is the pride. It will grant a guest, a challenger or a bearer of gifts what it would never grant a supplicant. Do not try to creep up on it; it hunts by nose. And when it calls up mist and fog, remember that the murk blinds it no less than you: go still, and it must guess.

sections.title: How it fights
sections.body: It fights like a soldier, not a brute. Cloud giants work in organised bands to a plan settled beforehand, and they will always take the higher ground if the ground offers it. The usual shape of it is a circle: they ring you at a distance and barrage you with stones while those with the sorcerous gift smother the field in mist and fog to break up your line, then close with the great morningstar, bulling and overrunning anyone still on their feet and knocking them sprawling. Expect griffons or great lions with them, and expect a priest or sorcerer somewhere behind.

sections.title: Margin notes
sections.body:
• Dress well. I am not joking — with these folk your coat argues before your mouth does.
• Its nose is better than its eyes. Downwind is worthless; go quiet and still inside its own fog instead.
• Kill the caster in the back rank first, or you will fight the whole band blind.

sections.title: Parley (wary)
sections.body: Talk, yes — but arrive as an equal or as a guest, never as a beggar. I dined in a cloud hall once and left with a harp string and my life; the second hall of that line kept the last man who tried it in a larder. Bring a gift, praise the music, and watch the host's rings.

lore.summary: A man-shape of smelted iron, smooth-featured and armoured, sometimes carrying a sword it has no need of. It makes no sound and gives off no smell, and it moves with a ponderous, oiled gait that sets the flagstones trembling at every step. Within it is a spirit of earth, bound unwilling into the metal and set to keep an order given long ago — usually across a doorway you wish to pass.

sections.title: Hunter's assessment
sections.body:
Size: Large — an iron man broader than a door and heavier than a warhorse in barding.
Durability: Very nearly unbreakable. You will be exhausted long before it is troubled.
Defenses: Proof against very nearly all sorcery, and ordinary steel skids from it. Only adamantine bites deep enough to matter.
Speed: Ponderous. It never hurries, because it never needs to.
Might: Fists like falling anvils, and a cloud of poisonous vapour breathed out at intervals that rots the strength out of a living body.
Mind: None whatever. No fear, no anger, no boredom, no judgement — nothing behind the face but the last command it was given.
Disposition: Wholly indifferent. It cannot be threatened, flattered, bribed, tricked or provoked; it stops when the order is discharged or the iron is broken.
Bane: Adamantine, and rust. Lesser metal is wasted on it and spells slide off, but a stroke of lightning leaves it sluggish and stumbling for a short while, and rust-magic or a rust-beast eats it exactly as it would eat any other iron. Never bring fire against it: flame not only mends the metal, it shakes off the sluggishness on the instant.

sections.title: How it fights
sections.body: There are no tactics in it. It walks at whatever its maker told it to walk at, hammers with both fists until the thing stops moving, and breathes its poison cloud whenever the breath is ready — it costs the golem nothing and it does not care who is standing in the vapour. It cannot be lured, feinted at, or driven off, and it will not pursue past the bound of its order unless the order says so. If it has no standing command and you strike it, it simply returns the blow, forever.

sections.title: Margin notes
sections.body:
• Adamantine or go home. Good steel only rings and tells it where you stand.
• The vapour kills more hunters than the fists. Hold your breath, back out of the cloud, come back in on the far side.
• I watched a wizard mend one with a fireball. He was very apologetic. Sheathe the flame.

sections.title: Parley (never)
sections.body: There is nobody home to answer. Speaking to one is speaking to a hinge. But the maker is a different matter entirely — the golem obeys a voice, and if you can find whose voice it is and treat with him, the iron stops without a single blow struck. That is the only conversation on offer.

sections.title: Special abilities
sections.body:
Breath Weapon (Su): 10-foot cube, cloud of poisonous gas lasting 1 round, free action once every 1d4+1 rounds; initial damage 1d4 Con, secondary damage 3d4 Con, Fortitude DC 19 negates. The save DC is Constitution-based.

Immunity to Magic (Ex): An iron golem is immune to any spell or spell-like ability that allows spell resistance. In addition, certain spells and effects function differently against it. A magical attack that deals electricity damage slows an iron golem (as the slow spell) for 3 rounds, with no saving throw. A magical attack that deals fire damage breaks any slow effect on the golem and heals 1 point of damage for each 3 points of damage the attack would otherwise deal; any healing beyond its full normal vigour is gained as temporary vigour instead. For example, an iron golem caught in a fireball that would deal 18 points of damage instead recovers 6 points. An iron golem gets no saving throw against fire effects. An iron golem is affected normally by rust attacks, such as that of a rust monster or a rusting grasp spell.

Construct Traits: A construct is an animated object or an artificially created creature. It has no Constitution score, darkvision 60 ft. and low-light vision, and immunity to all mind-affecting effects (charms, compulsions, phantasms, patterns and morale effects). It is immune to poison, sleep effects, paralysis, stunning, disease, death effects and necromancy effects, and is not subject to critical hits, nonlethal damage, ability damage, ability drain, fatigue, exhaustion or energy drain. It is immune to any effect requiring a Fortitude save unless that effect also works on objects or is harmless. It cannot heal damage on its own, though it can be repaired through the Craft Construct feat or spells such as make whole. It is not at risk of death from massive damage, but is destroyed outright the instant its vitality is exhausted. It cannot be raised or resurrected, and it does not eat, sleep or breathe.

Description: An iron golem has a humanoid body made from iron and almost always displays armour of some sort; its features are much smoother than those of a stone golem, and it sometimes carries a short sword in one hand. It stands 12 feet tall and weighs about 5,000 pounds. It cannot speak or make any vocal noise, nor does it have any distinguishable odour, and each ponderous step causes the floor to tremble unless it is on a thick, solid foundation.

lore.summary: Chiselled whole from a single block of hard stone and stylised to the vanity of its maker — armour carved into the shoulders, a sigil cut deep in the breast, patterns worked down the limbs. It stands where it was set, in vault doors and tomb halls and the deep rooms of guarded towers, without hunger or boredom, until someone crosses the line it was told to hold.

sections.title: Hunter's assessment
sections.body:
Size: Large — a carved man taller than a mounted rider and heavier than the horse.
Durability: Formidable. Stone does not tire, bleed, or reconsider.
Defenses: Proof against very nearly all sorcery, and a hide of hard stone that turns any blade short of adamantine.
Speed: Slow and grinding. It walks; it does not chase.
Might: Two granite fists, each blow like a falling lintel, and a will that drags at the air around it so that everyone near moves as though wading.
Mind: None at all. It has no thought, no strategy, and nothing you can say will reach it.
Disposition: Utterly emotionless and impossible to provoke. It does the last thing it was told and nothing else, and it does it patiently for as long as the stone lasts.
Bane: Adamantine to cut it, and the earth-magic that softens rock into mud, which leaves it dragging and helpless for a good while with no chance to shrug it off. The working that turns stone to flesh strips away both its guard and its proof against spells for a single breath — have every blow and every spell ready for that heartbeat. Above all, never let anyone cast the hardening of mud into rock near it: that makes the thing whole again.

sections.title: How it fights
sections.body: It closes at its own grinding pace and pounds with both fists, and there is no more art to it than that. What makes it dangerous is the pull it exerts: every so often the air around it thickens, and anyone caught in that near circle finds their arms and legs slowed to half a purpose, unable to strike twice or step away clean. That is when the fists land. It will not flank, will not feint, will not choose a target more cleverly than nearest — but it also will not stop, and it will fight in an antimagic field as happily as anywhere.

sections.title: Margin notes
sections.body:
• The dragging weight is the trap, not the fists. Fight it from outside that near circle and step in only to strike.
• Adamantine, a mason's maul, or the earth-magic that turns rock soft. Everything else is noise.
• Read the sigil on its breast. Twice now that carving has told me whose house I was really robbing.

sections.title: Parley (never)
sections.body: Nothing there to talk to — no more than a portcullis. Strike, or leave. But somebody carved that sigil on its chest, and somebody told it where to stand: find that one, and you may walk through the door without lifting a hammer. Treat with the sculptor, never the sculpture.

A transmute rock to mud spell slows a stone golem (as the slow spell) for 2d6 rounds, with no saving throw, while transmute mud to rock restores it to full vigour, repairing all the damage it has taken. A stone to flesh spell does not actually change the golem’s structure, but negates its damage reduction and immunity to magic for 1 full round.

Construct Traits: A construct is an animated object or an artificially created creature. It has no Constitution score, darkvision 60 ft. and low-light vision, and immunity to all mind-affecting effects (charms, compulsions, phantasms, patterns and morale effects). It is immune to poison, sleep effects, paralysis, stunning, disease, death effects and necromancy effects, and is not subject to critical hits, nonlethal damage, ability damage, ability drain, fatigue, exhaustion or energy drain. It is immune to any effect requiring a Fortitude save unless that effect also works on objects or is harmless. It cannot heal damage on its own, though it can be repaired through the Craft Construct feat or spells such as make whole. It is not at risk of death from massive damage, but is destroyed outright the instant its vitality is exhausted. It cannot be raised or resurrected, and it does not eat, sleep or breathe.

Description: A stone golem has a humanoid body chiselled from stone, stands 9 feet tall and weighs around 2,000 pounds. Its body is frequently stylised to suit its creator — it might appear to wear armour with a particular symbol carved on the breastplate, or have designs worked into the stone of its limbs. Stone golems are formidable opponents, being physically powerful and difficult to harm.

lore.summary: A ghoulish patchwork of stolen limbs and torso, sewn from a half-dozen graves and shocked into motion. It stands hunched and stiff-jointed, as though it were never quite the master of its own arms, and speaks only in a hoarse roar. No natural beast will willingly follow its trail. You find them in the cellars of surgeons who mistook cleverness for wisdom.

sections.title: Hunter's assessment
sections.body:
Size: Large — taller than any man, though lighter than it looks; there is little in it but meat and thread.
Durability: Tough and untiring, but the least durable of its kind. Dead flesh feels nothing and keeps working.
Defenses: Proof against very nearly all sorcery, and a rubbery, stitched hide that shrugs off lesser weapons — adamantine tells, ordinary steel less so.
Speed: Quicker than any golem of stone or iron; it walks at a living man's pace and will follow you across a room in a stride or two.
Might: Great strength badly governed — two hammering fists that smash bone through mail, delivered with no more skill than a falling beam.
Mind: Nothing but the bound spirit, and that spirit is not obedient by nature. It has no thoughts, only orders it is straining against.
Disposition: Blank until roused, then relentless. The longer a fight runs the likelier the spirit is to slip its leash and rampage at whatever stands nearest.
Bane: Adamantine cuts it best. Fire and frost both leave it slowed and stumbling, and that is the surest handle any hunter has on the thing — either will serve. Keep lightning sheathed: a storm-stroke mends it and shakes the slowness straight off. And give it time to go berserk: once loose it strikes whatever is closest, its maker included.

sections.title: How it fights
sections.body: It wades in and hammers, nothing more. There is no craft in it at all — no guard, no footwork, no notion of which of you is the greater danger — but the blows land like a smith's and it does not stop for wounds. The thing to watch for is the moment the bound spirit tears free. Then all direction leaves it: it rampages, mauling the nearest living creature or smashing whatever it can lift if nobody is in reach, and moves on to wreck something else. Its maker can shout it back under control, but only if he is close, calm and very persuasive.

sections.title: Margin notes
sections.body:
• Fire or frost, either one, and it staggers. Keep every storm-spell sheathed — lightning feeds it.
• Let a long fight run and step wide. Twice I have won by letting the thing turn on the man who sewed it.
• Your horse and hounds will not go near it, and they are right. Leave them well back or lose them.

sections.title: Parley (never)
sections.body: Nothing in there to bargain with — only a furious spirit stitched into somebody's grandfather. It cannot hear a word of what you say. The maker can, though, and he is usually the shaking man in the corner. Talk to him, and do it before the thing goes berserk and settles the matter for both of you.

sections.title: Special abilities
sections.body:
Berserk (Ex): When a flesh golem enters combat, there is a cumulative 1% chance each round that its elemental spirit breaks free and the golem goes berserk. The uncontrolled golem goes on a rampage, attacking the nearest living creature or smashing some object smaller than itself if no creature is within reach, then moving on to spread more destruction. The golem’s creator, if within 60 feet, can try to regain control by speaking firmly and persuasively to the golem, which requires a DC 19 Charisma check. It takes 1 minute of inactivity by the golem to reset its berserk chance to 0%.

Immunity to Magic (Ex): A flesh golem is immune to any spell or spell-like ability that allows spell resistance. In addition, certain spells and effects function differently against it. A magical attack that deals cold or fire damage slows a flesh golem (as the slow spell) for 2d6 rounds, with no saving throw. A magical attack that deals electricity damage breaks any slow effect on the golem and heals 1 point of damage for every 3 points of damage the attack would otherwise deal; any healing beyond its full normal vigour is gained as temporary vigour instead. For example, a flesh golem struck by a lightning bolt that would have dealt 11 points of damage instead recovers 3 points. A flesh golem gets no saving throw against attacks that deal electricity damage.

Construct Traits: A construct is an animated object or an artificially created creature. It has no Constitution score, darkvision 60 ft. and low-light vision, and immunity to all mind-affecting effects (charms, compulsions, phantasms, patterns and morale effects). It is immune to poison, sleep effects, paralysis, stunning, disease, death effects and necromancy effects, and is not subject to critical hits, nonlethal damage, ability damage, ability drain, fatigue, exhaustion or energy drain. It is immune to any effect requiring a Fortitude save unless that effect also works on objects or is harmless. It cannot heal damage on its own, though it can be repaired through the Craft Construct feat or spells such as make whole. It is not at risk of death from massive damage, but is destroyed outright the instant its vitality is exhausted. It cannot be raised or resurrected, and it does not eat, sleep or breathe.

Description: A flesh golem is a ghoulish collection of stolen humanoid body parts stitched together into a single composite form. No natural animal willingly tracks a flesh golem. It stands 8 feet tall and weighs almost 500 pounds, wears whatever clothing its creator desires (usually just a ragged pair of trousers) and carries no possessions or weapons. It cannot speak, although it can emit a hoarse roar of sorts, and it walks with a stiff-jointed gait, as if not in complete control of its body.

lore.summary: Priests raise these, not wizards. A block of river clay is sculpted into a broad man's shape, cured with rare oils and powders, and an elemental spirit is bound inside it by prayer. It guards tomb and treasury without hunger, sleep or mercy, and the hurts it deals do not close. Sooner or later the spirit slips its collar, and then it kills whatever stands nearest.

sections.title: Hunter's assessment
sections.body:
Size: Large — a heavy, thickset figure of baked clay, naked but for a stiff band of leather or metal about its hips.
Durability: Enormously tough. It does not tire, does not bleed, and fights on ruined until it is rubble.
Defenses: Blade and arrow scarcely mark it, and it sheds nearly all sorcery outright; acid flung at it only feeds the clay and mends what you have broken.
Speed: A slow, clumsy gait — until it quickens itself, once in a day, and comes on faster than a man can back away.
Might: Two crushing slams. The wounds they leave fester, refuse to knit, and turn aside the healing prayers of all but the strongest priest.
Mind: None whatever. No wits, no speech, no voice of any kind — it cannot so much as grunt. Only the last order it was given.
Disposition: Obedient to its maker's word and wholly without malice, until the bound spirit tears loose. Then it rampages, smashing whatever lives or stands, and no craft yet known can rein it in again.
Bane: An adamantine hammer, or nothing — it wants both the weight and the rare metal. Where spells fail, the old earth-workings bite: the charm that shifts earth hurls it back and batters it, the ray that unmakes slows it to a crawl, and a called quaking of the ground pins it where it stands.

sections.title: How it fights
sections.body: It comes on straight, without guile, slamming with both fists and stopping for nothing. After the first exchange it may quicken itself and land blows twice as thick. It never flanks, never feints, never flees; it walks through your line toward whatever its master named, and the wounds it leaves stay open behind it while your healer's words come to nothing.

sections.title: Margin notes
sections.body:
• An adamantine hammer or nothing. Your good sword will only ring off it.
• Do not throw acid at it. I watched a wizard mend one for us. He is buried under it.
• Its hurts will not close for prayer or poultice. Break off while your people still have blood in them.

sections.title: Parley (never)
sections.body: There is nothing there to speak to. I have shouted the true name of a golem's maker at one in three tongues; it broke my shield arm on the third. Talk to the priest who owns it, if he still lives. If the spirit has already slipped free, talk to no one and run.

sections.body: Grave — A grave peril

sections.title: Special abilities
sections.body:
Berserk (Ex): When a clay golem enters combat, there is a cumulative 1% chance each round that its elemental spirit breaks free and the golem goes berserk. The uncontrolled golem goes on a rampage, attacking the nearest living creature or smashing some object smaller than itself if no creature is within reach, then moving on to spread more destruction. Once a clay golem goes berserk, no known method can re-establish control.

Cursed Wound (Ex): The damage a clay golem deals doesn’t heal naturally and resists healing spells. A character attempting to cast a conjuration (healing) spell on a creature damaged by a clay golem must succeed on a DC 26 caster level check, or the spell has no effect on the injured character.

Haste (Su): After it has engaged in at least 1 round of combat, a clay golem can haste itself once per day as a free action. The effect lasts 3 rounds and is otherwise the same as the spell.

Immunity to Magic (Ex): A clay golem is immune to any spell or spell-like ability that allows spell resistance. In addition, certain spells and effects function differently against it. A move earth spell drives the golem back 120 feet and deals 3d12 points of damage to it. A disintegrate spell slows the golem (as the slow spell) for 1d6 rounds and deals 1d12 points of damage. An earthquake spell cast directly at a clay golem stops it from moving on its next turn and deals 5d10 points of damage. The golem gets no saving throw against any of these effects. Any magical attack that deals acid damage heals 1 point of damage for every 3 points of damage it would otherwise deal; any healing beyond its full normal vigour is gained as temporary vigour instead. For example, a clay golem caught in the breath weapon of a black dragon that would have dealt 22 points of damage instead recovers 7 points. A clay golem gets no saving throw against magical attacks that deal acid damage.

Construct Traits: A construct is an animated object or an artificially created creature. It has no Constitution score, darkvision 60 ft. and low-light vision, and immunity to all mind-affecting effects (charms, compulsions, phantasms, patterns and morale effects). It is immune to poison, sleep effects, paralysis, stunning, disease, death effects and necromancy effects, and is not subject to critical hits, nonlethal damage, ability damage, ability drain, fatigue, exhaustion or energy drain. It is immune to any effect requiring a Fortitude save unless that effect also works on objects or is harmless. It cannot heal damage on its own, though it can be repaired through the Craft Construct feat or spells such as make whole. It is not at risk of death from massive damage, but is destroyed outright the instant its vitality is exhausted. It cannot be raised or resurrected, and it does not eat, sleep or breathe.

Description: A clay golem has a humanoid body made from clay and wears no clothing except a metal or stiff leather garment around its hips. It cannot speak or make any vocal noise, weighs around 600 pounds, and walks and moves with a slow, clumsy gait.

lore.summary: The greatest of the demons and the captains of the Abyss's armies. A horned giant of a thing, dark red, wings like a storm-front, wreathed head to heel in standing fire, with a many-tailed burning whip in one fist and a sword like a bolt of lightning in the other. It commands lesser demons by the horde and steps across the world at a whim. Most hunters meet one only once.

sections.title: Hunter's assessment
sections.body:
Size: Large — half again the height of a tall man and vastly heavier, with a wingspan that fills a hall.
Durability: Beyond nearly anything that walks. You will not grind it down; you must undo it.
Defenses: Fire, lightning and venom do nothing at all; frost and acid little. Common steel is wasted on it, most spells slough away unfelt, and it sees through every veil, disguise and darkness without pause.
Speed: Swift afoot, swifter on the wing, and gone from one place to another the instant a fight stops amusing it.
Might: A sword that takes a head off clean at a touch, and a whip of hooks and burning tails that snares a man and drags him against that blazing body to cook there. Where its arms will not serve, it calls down storms of fire, madness, a word that stops the heart — and fresh demons to hold your flanks.
Mind: Cunning as any archmage and older than your kingdom. It reasons, it plans, it lies beautifully, and it speaks straight into your skull without moving its jaw.
Disposition: Cruel without floor or limit, loyal to nothing, faithless even to its own kind. It fights at a distance while that suits, closes when it grows bored, and would sooner unmake your mind than your body.
Bane: Cold iron, or steel hallowed for good — nothing else bites deep, and holy power grieves it. Know this before you strike the last blow: it dies in a blast of white fire that has killed more hunters than the demon itself. Slay it from as far off as you can contrive, and never with a blade you mean to keep.

sections.title: How it fights
sections.body: It opens from the air and from range: an unholy pall over itself, then fire poured across your line, or a word that folds a man in on himself, or a horde of lesser demons summoned to pin you while it works. Then madness, then a word that stuns. Only when you are ragged does it come to arms — sword and whip together, snaring one of you against its burning body — and the moment the fight turns it steps away, mends its distance, and begins the whole cruel order again.

sections.title: Margin notes
sections.body:
• Cold iron, or blessed steel. Anything else is a stick you are holding.
• When it falls, be far off and flat. Its dying took my second company entire.
• It will not fight fair. Expect fire from the sky, then find it standing behind your archers.

sections.title: Parley (wary)
sections.body: Words are possible — it speaks into the mind in any tongue and is clever enough to enjoy them. But understand why it consents. I bargained with one on the Blasted Stair for the better part of an hour; it was savouring me. Say your piece, learn what you came for, and be gone before it finishes tasting.

sections.title: Threat
sections.body: Legendary — A legendary terror

sections.title: Stat block (SRD)
sections.body:

Initiative: +11

sections.title: Special abilities
sections.body:
Death Throes (Ex): When killed, a balor explodes in a blinding flash of light that deals 100 points of damage to anything within 100 feet (Reflex DC 30 half). This explosion automatically destroys any weapons the balor is holding. The save DC is Constitution-based.

Vorpal Sword (Su): Every balor carries a +1 vorpal longsword that looks like a flame or a bolt of lightning. On a successful critical hit the vorpal weapon severs the opponent's head from its body.

Entangle (Ex): A balor's +1 flaming whip entangles foes much like an attack with a net. The whip is destroyed after taking 20 points of damage. The whip needs no folding. If it hits, the target and the balor immediately make opposed Strength checks; if the balor wins, it drags the target against its flaming body. The target remains anchored against the balor's body until it escapes the whip. The whip is a long, flexible weapon with many tails tipped with hooks, spikes, and balls, dealing bludgeoning and slashing damage in addition to fire damage. Its reach is 20 feet.

Flaming Body (Su): The body of a balor is wreathed in flame. Anyone grappling a balor takes 6d6 points of fire damage each round.

Spell-Like Abilities: At will—blasphemy (DC 25), dominate monster (DC 27), greater dispel magic, greater teleport (self plus 50 pounds of objects only), insanity (DC 25), power word stun, telekinesis (DC 23), unholy aura (DC 26); 1/day—fire storm (DC 26), implosion (DC 27). Caster level 20th. The save DCs are Charisma-based.

Summon Demon (Sp): Once per day a balor can automatically summon 4d10 dretches, 1d4 hezrous, or one nalfeshnee, glabrezu, marilith, or balor. This ability is the equivalent of a 9th-level spell.

True Seeing (Su): Balors have a continuous true seeing ability, as the spell (caster level 20th).

Aligned Weapons (Ex): A balor's natural weapons, as well as any weapons it wields, are treated as chaotic-aligned and evil-aligned for the purpose of overcoming damage reduction.

Skills: Balors have a +8 racial bonus on Listen and Spot checks.

Size and Appearance: A balor stands about 12 feet tall. Its skin is usually dark red. It weighs about 4,500 pounds.

lore.summary: The greatest of the devils, and the finest lawyers in creation. Twice the height of a man, red-scaled, horned and tailed, wrapped in vast wings it wears like a grotesque cloak; flame stands about it and dread rolls off it as cold rolls off ice. Pit fiends command legions of lesser devils and hold the signed word of a great many clever men who thought themselves cleverer.

sections.title: Hunter's assessment
sections.body:
Size: Large — a red giant of a devil, fanged and crowned with horns, its wings folded round it like a cloak until the moment they are not.
Durability: Terrible. Cut it and it knits itself whole while you watch, faster than you can open it again.
Defenses: Fire and venom are nothing to it, frost and acid nearly so. It sees in any dark, natural or conjured, sheds most spells, and can go unseen whenever it pleases.
Speed: Quick on the ground, sure in the air, and across the world in a breath when it chooses to be.
Might: Claws, wings, tail and jaws all in the same heartbeat; the tail coils and crushes, and the bite carries both a killing venom and a wasting sickness that eats a man's strength away over days. It throws fire as a boy throws stones and can pull down a rain of burning stars. Once in a long while it can grant a true wish, and that is the hook on which it hangs kingdoms.
Mind: Brilliant, patient, and ordered as a ledger. It remembers every word you said and the exact shape of every promise you made.
Disposition: Lawful and utterly evil, which is the worst pairing there is. It would rather have you bound by your own signature than broken by its hands, and it has all the time there is to wait.
Bane: Silvered steel that has been hallowed for good, or holy power outright — nothing less keeps its flesh from closing. Fight it in company, for the dread alone routs lone men. And never, on any terms, put your name to anything.

sections.title: How it fights
sections.body: It prepares before you know it is there: an unholy pall, its dread let loose across the room, devils called up to hold your flanks. Then fire in a burst, then a working that freezes half your company in place, then the falling stars. Only after that does it wade in, and it goes straight for whoever is already bleeding — claws, wings, tail and teeth at once, the tail coiling to crush. Endangered, it simply steps out of the world and comes back rested.

sections.title: Margin notes
sections.body:
• Silver, and blessed. Plain silver is a courtesy, not a weapon.
• Do not sign. Do not nod. Do not say 'agreed' anywhere it can hear you.
• The chills its teeth give you take a week to kill. Find a temple well before then.

sections.title: Parley (wary)
sections.body: It will talk, and it will keep every word of the bargain and none of its meaning. I have struck two agreements with devils and regretted both, though I read each aloud twice. Speak plainly, promise nothing, name no third party, and carry home only what you carried in.

sections.body: Legendary — A legendary adversary
