sections.title: Special abilities
sections.body:
Combat: A phantom fungus usually roams quietly, hunting for prey. It attacks lone individuals almost anywhere, but when tackling groups it prefers an open space where it has a better chance.

Greater Invisibility (Su): This ability is constant, allowing a phantom fungus to remain invisible even when attacking. It works like greater invisibility (caster level 12th) and lasts as long as the phantom fungus is alive. This ability is not subject to the invisibility purge spell. A phantom fungus becomes visible 1 minute after it is killed.

Skills: A phantom fungus has a +5 racial bonus on Move Silently checks.

Plant Traits (Ex): A phantom fungus is immune to all mind-affecting effects, to poison, sleep effects, paralysis, polymorph and stunning, and is not subject to critical hits. It cannot be raised or resurrected, and it has low-light vision.

lore.summary: A purple stalk that cannot move, cannot strike and cannot be reasoned with — and it has killed more lamp-carrying fools than half the beasts in this book. Bring light or movement near a shrieker and it screams, on and on, and every hungry thing in earshot comes to see what the noise has caught. It is a dinner bell, and you are the dinner.

sections.title: Hunter's assessment
sections.body:
Size: Medium — a fleshy purple stalk about the height of a kneeling man.
Durability: Feeble. One honest stroke generally ends it.
Defenses: None to speak of. It cannot dodge, it cannot flinch, and it has neither fear nor sleep nor venom to trouble it. Its only armour is whatever answers the noise — and the neighbouring fungi's poison does not trouble it either.
Speed: Rooted. It has never taken a step in its life and never will.
Might: None at all. It has no attack of any kind. Every death it causes is dealt by somebody else's teeth.
Mind: Nothing. It does not know that you are there — only that something is.
Disposition: Blindly reactive. Light or movement close by sets it wailing for a good while, and it does not care in the least who answers.
Bane: It cannot chase, and it cannot fight. Hood the lantern, move slow and wide of it, or kill it fast and quiet before the sound carries far. Dead, it is only a mushroom.

sections.title: How it fights
sections.body: It does not fight. It shrieks — a piercing wail that runs on well past the point of bearing — and whatever comes running does the fighting for it. Violet fungi grow among them for exactly that reason, untroubled by each other, and the local predators have learned that the racket means meat.

sections.title: Margin notes
sections.body:
• Hood the lantern before the passage, not after. It answers to light as readily as to footfalls.
• Kill it in one stroke or leave it be. A wounded shrieker wails just as loud as a hale one.
• Where they grow in a patch, look for violet fungi among them. The noise is the bait; the tentacles are the trap.

sections.title: Parley (never)
sections.body: There is nobody home. But I will say this much for the shrieker: it is honest. It tells the whole cavern exactly what it thinks of you, at the top of its voice, and it never once pretended otherwise. Kill it quickly and say nothing over it.

sections.title: Threat
sections.body: Minor — A minor peril, and a loud one

sections.title: Stat block (SRD)
sections.body:

Full Attack: —

Special Qualities: Low-light vision, plant traits

Skills: —
Feats: —
Environment: Underground

Alignment: Always neutral

sections.title: Special abilities
sections.body:
Shriekers and Violet Fungi: Shriekers and violet fungi often work together to attract and kill prey. When the shriekers' hellish racket attracts a curious creature, the violet fungus tries to kill it. Both creatures enjoy the fruits of a successful hunt.

Description: A shrieker is a stationary fungus that emits a loud noise to attract prey or when disturbed. Shriekers live in dark, subterranean places, often in the company of violet fungi, whose poison they are immune to. Shriekers come in shades of purple.

Combat: A shrieker has no means of attack. Instead, it lures prey to its vicinity by emitting a loud noise.

Shriek (Ex): Movement or a light source within 10 feet of a shrieker causes the fungus to emit a piercing sound that lasts for 1d3 rounds. The sound attracts nearby creatures that are disposed to investigate it. Some creatures that live near shriekers come to learn that the fungus's noise means there is food nearby.

Plant Traits (Ex): A shrieker is immune to all mind-affecting effects, to poison, sleep effects, paralysis, polymorph and stunning, and is not subject to critical hits. It cannot be raised or resurrected, and it has low-light vision.

lore.summary: Purple all over, or dull grey stippled with purple, and to a tired eye no different from the shrieker beside it. That is the whole of the trick. The violet fungus grows among the screamers and lets them do the calling; when the curious arrive, it lashes out with rubbery arms whose touch rots the strength out of a man. Both plants feed on what falls.

sections.title: Hunter's assessment
sections.body:
Size: Medium — a squat purple cap, no taller than the shrieker it hides among and easily mistaken for one.
Durability: Modest. Hardier than its screaming neighbour, but it will not stand long against a good blade.
Defenses: No armour worth the name, and none needed. Plant-blank: fear, charm, sleep, venom and the seizing of limbs all slide off it, and there are no vitals in it to find.
Speed: It shuffles, very slowly — slowly enough that it scarcely counts. But do not take it for rooted the way its neighbour is.
Might: A crown of rubbery arms that flail at anything living, and they reach a good deal further than the plant appears to stand.
Mind: None. It is an appetite on a stalk. It cannot be startled, bribed, or bluffed.
Disposition: It does not hunt. It waits, usually among shriekers, and lashes whatever wanders into reach.
Bane: It has no answer at all to reach. Spear, polearm, sling and bow undo it entirely. Its rot works only through broken skin, so gauntlets and closed sleeves spare you the worst — but carry something for the wasting afterward.

sections.title: How it fights
sections.body: It flails, and goes on flailing, at everything living in reach — no cunning, no chosen target, no let-up. The venom on those arms works only where the skin is opened, and it takes you twice: once at the touch, and again a while later, sapping the strength from your arms and the wind from your chest both times.

sections.title: Margin notes
sections.body:
• Count the arms before you step in. Shrieker and violet fungus look the same until one of them reaches for you.
• Kill it with a length of wood between you. It has no answer whatever to a spear.
• The rot comes twice, once at the wound and once well after. If your grip is failing when the fight is over, you are not done being poisoned.

sections.title: Parley (never)
sections.body: Nothing to address. The only conversation I have ever had in a fungus patch was with myself, aloud, tallying which purple stalks had arms and which did not. Do that tallying from further off than you think you need to.

sections.title: Threat

sections.title: Special abilities
sections.body:
Shriekers and Violet Fungi: Shriekers and violet fungi often work together to attract and kill prey. When the shriekers' hellish racket attracts a curious creature, the violet fungus tries to kill it. Both creatures enjoy the fruits of a successful hunt.

Description: Violet fungi resemble shriekers and are often found growing among them. A violet fungus's coloration ranges from purple overall to dull gray or violet covered with purple spots.

Combat: A violet fungus flails about with its tentacles at living creatures that come within its reach.

Poison (Ex): Injury, Fortitude DC 14, initial and secondary damage 1d4 Str and 1d4 Con. The save DC is Constitution-based.

Plant Traits (Ex): A violet fungus is immune to all mind-affecting effects, to poison, sleep effects, paralysis, polymorph and stunning, and is not subject to critical hits. It cannot be raised or resurrected, and it has low-light vision.

lore.summary: A spreading sheet of inky filth that lives only to eat, and eats very nearly everything. It climbs sheer walls, hangs from ceilings and drips down on whatever passes beneath, following warmth by scent and tremor through the deep places. Its touch ruins mail, harness, haft and flesh alike; only stone stands against it.

sections.title: Hunter's assessment
sections.body:
Size: Huge — a black sheet broad as a cottage floor and no thicker than a man's forearm.
Durability: Enormous. It has no organs to spoil and no blood to lose; it simply keeps coming.
Defenses: Cut it and you do not wound it, you make two of it. It cannot be poisoned, frightened, charmed or put to sleep, and there is nothing on it to strike at cleanly.
Speed: Slow on the flat, but it walks up bare stone as easily as it crosses it, and it never tires.
Might: It slams, takes hold, wraps and squeezes — and every moment of contact is a burning.
Mind: None whatever. No thought to read, no fear to work upon, no will to bend.
Disposition: Hunger without malice. It attacks whatever it meets and eats what it stops.
Bane: Its acid has no power over stone, and it senses only a short way about itself. Fight from bare rock, carry nothing you cannot afford to lose, and beat it down with a stone maul, flame or spellcraft — never with an edge.

sections.title: How it fights
sections.body: It feels your step through the floor, flows down a wall or across the passage, and lays a limb of itself over you. Once it has hold it wraps and squeezes, and the squeezing is a burning: mail, straps, boots and the weapon in your fist all go to slime while it works. Strike it with edge or point and the piece you cut away rises as a second pudding with the same appetite. Only stone comes out of it whole.

sections.title: Margin notes
sections.body:
• Leave the good sword sheathed. Cutting it only buys you another one.
• Stone is safe from it. Your buckles, your axe-haft and your boots are not — fight on bare rock and expect to walk home barefoot.
• It comes from above. Look up before you look ahead.

sections.title: Parley (never)
sections.body: There is nothing there to speak to. I have shouted at one, offered it meat, offered it coin, stood as still as a post and let it come — it came all the same. No ears, and no thought behind them. Do not spend breath; spend the time putting stone and distance between you.

sections.body: Grave — A grave peril

sections.title: Special abilities
sections.body:
Acid (Ex): The creature secretes a digestive acid that dissolves organic material and metal quickly, but does not affect stone. Any melee hit or constrict attack deals acid damage, and the opponent's armour and clothing dissolve and become useless immediately unless they succeed on DC 21 Reflex saves. A metal or wooden weapon that strikes a black pudding also dissolves immediately unless it succeeds on a DC 21 Reflex save. The save DCs are Constitution-based. The pudding's acidic touch deals 21 points of damage per round to wooden or metal objects, but the ooze must remain in contact with the object for 1 full round to deal this damage.

Constrict (Ex): A black pudding deals automatic slam and acid damage with a successful grapple check. The opponent's clothing and armour take a –4 penalty on Reflex saves against the acid.

Improved Grab (Ex): To use this ability, a black pudding must hit with its slam attack. It can then attempt to start a grapple as a free action without provoking an attack of opportunity. If it wins the grapple check, it establishes a hold and can constrict.

Split (Ex): Slashing and piercing weapons deal no damage to a black pudding. Instead the creature splits into two identical puddings, each with half of the original's remaining vigour (round down). A pudding worn down to its last 10 points of vigour cannot be split further, and it is destroyed once that remainder is gone.

Ooze Traits (Ex): Mindless: no Intelligence score, and immunity to all mind-affecting effects (charms, compulsions, phantasms, patterns, and morale effects). Blind, but possessed of blindsight, with immunity to gaze attacks, visual effects, illusions, and other attack forms that rely on sight. Immunity to poison, sleep effects, paralysis, polymorph, and stunning. Not subject to critical hits or flanking. Proficient with its natural weapons only, and with no armour. Oozes eat and breathe, but do not sleep.

Skills: A black pudding has a +8 racial bonus on Climb checks and can always choose to take 10 on a Climb check, even if rushed or threatened.

Size: The typical black pudding measures 15 feet across and 2 feet thick. It weighs about 18,000 pounds.

lore.summary: A gray ooze looks like nothing at all — a slick of wet stone, a patch of old slime on a flagstone, a rotting log in the reeds. It lies flat and patient until warmth crosses it, then rears and strikes like an adder and folds itself about whatever it caught. Look for it in cold marshes, and in the damp under-halls where the fen creeps indoors.

sections.title: Hunter's assessment
sections.body:
Size: Medium — a spreading puddle no thicker than a hand's breadth, wider than a man is tall when it stretches.
Durability: Tougher than so small a thing has any right to be; it soaks up a deal of punishment before it stops.
Defenses: Frost cannot touch it and fire will not either — I wasted a good flask of oil proving as much. Poison and sleep are likewise nothing to it, and it is near invisible until it moves.
Speed: Very slow. It crawls, and unlike its kin it cannot climb.
Might: It strikes like a snake, takes hold and crushes, and the grip eats what it holds.
Mind: None. A stomach with no head upon it.
Disposition: It does not hunt so much as wait. Anything warm that blunders onto it is a meal.
Bane: Slower than a walking man and blind past a few paces — you can simply leave. Its acid has no power over stone, so stand on bare rock, and finish it with spellcraft, a stone-headed club, or an edge you are content to lose.

sections.title: How it fights
sections.body: It waits flat and unremarkable until something warm passes over it, then rears and slams down like a striking adder. What it hits it holds; what it holds it wraps and crushes, and the crushing burns away armour, straps and the sword in your hand together. Unlike the black pudding it does not divide when cut — but the blade that cuts it seldom survives the stroke, and neither torch nor frost will spare you the trade.

sections.title: Margin notes
sections.body:
• Poke the ground ahead with a stick in wet stone country. You will lose sticks. Better than boots.
• Save your oil and your frost — it feels neither. Rock and blunt weight, or a spell.
• You may cut it; it will not divide. Only know the blade is spent when you do.

sections.title: Parley (never)
sections.body: Nothing to say, and nothing there to hear it. I once spent a good quarter-hour speaking gently to what I took for a hurt beast lying in the reeds. It was this. It answered by taking my greaves, and most of one boot with them.

lore.summary: A great amber sheet, soft as spilled honey and far quicker than it looks. The ochre jelly climbs walls and ceilings and pours itself through any crack a coin would pass — under a barred door, down a murder-hole, into a locked strongroom. It wants meat and only meat. Your gear will come out of it whole; you will not.

sections.title: Hunter's assessment
sections.body:
Size: Large — a broad amber sheet, thin as a platter, that can squeeze itself into a crack no wider than a finger.
Durability: Stubborn. It endures a great deal, and much of what you do to it only makes more of it.
Defenses: Blade, point and lightning all fail — each stroke merely carves it in two and both halves come on. It cannot be poisoned, charmed, frightened or put to sleep.
Speed: Slow across open ground, but it climbs as readily as it crawls and reaches you from a ceiling or through a gap you believed secure.
Might: It flows over a man, takes hold and squeezes, and the touch of it eats the flesh away beneath.
Mind: None. Appetite in a puddle.
Disposition: Wholly indiscriminate. It moves toward warm meat, and nothing else in the world interests it.
Bane: Its acid works upon flesh alone — it will not harm metal, wood or stone. So armour genuinely serves here, and a maul or hammer serves better still. Keep the edges and the lightning sheathed and pound it flat.

sections.title: How it fights
sections.body: It feels the tremor of your step, flows over the floor or drops from above, and lays itself across you. Once it has hold it constricts, and the constriction is a slow burning of the skin beneath the harness. Cut it, stab it, or touch it with lightning and you have merely made two jellies of one appetite; both take hold at once, and the hunter who keeps hacking is shortly fighting a crowd of his own making.

sections.title: Margin notes
sections.body:
• Mace, hammer, staff. Every cut you land makes another one of it.
• No lightning. I watched a young wizard turn one jelly into four with a single stroke and then run out of ideas.
• Your mail is safe from it; you are not. Keep it buckled and keep it off your skin.

sections.title: Parley (never)
sections.body: A honeyed sheet with no more mind than honey. I have watched one flow past a shouting man to reach a dead goat, finish the goat, and then come back for the man at the same idle pace. Words are wasted on it. All it hears is footfalls.

lore.summary: Giant ants keep hives as their small kin do, and the hive is the whole of the matter: workers to dig and carry, soldiers to hold the road, and one great queen in the dark below who is the reason for all of it. They run fast over the grasslands, climb well, and follow a scent as surely as a hound. Meet one, and you have not met one.

sections.title: Hunter's assessment
sections.body:
Size: Workers and soldiers run about as long as a man is tall; the queen half again as long and heavier than a pony.
Durability: Each is well plated in shell and takes some killing — and there are always more of them than you counted.
Defenses: Hard chitin over the whole of it, and nothing magical at all. The numbers do the work that armour cannot.
Speed: Very fast over open ground and quick up a wall or a tree trunk. You will not outrun a soldier on the grass.
Might: Shearing jaws that take hold and will not let go. The soldier carries a sting in its tail besides, and the sting spits a burning fluid into the wound it makes.
Mind: None. They neither learn nor fear nor break; they follow the scent and the hive and nothing else.
Disposition: Indifferent until the hive is threatened or the smell of meat crosses them. Then wholly implacable.
Bane: No wit at all. A false scent, a burning brand drawn across the trail, or a plugged tunnel mouth confuses them entirely. Take the soldiers at the entrance where only a few can reach you, and never go down after the queen without fire and a way out.

sections.title: How it fights
sections.body: Soldiers come out to meet you at the mouth of the hive and bite to hold. Once a soldier has hold, it curls its abdomen round and drives the sting home again and again, and the sting burns as it pierces. Workers fight poorly but swarm in to bite and drag, and they keep arriving out of the dark for as long as you stand there. The queen fights only in her own chamber, biting and holding you fast while everything left in the hive comes down the tunnel at your back.

sections.title: Margin notes
sections.body:
• Their nose beats their eyes. Cross running water, or drag something ranker than yourself behind you.
• Fight at the tunnel mouth. Inside they come at you from every side and from overhead.
• The soldier's sting burns as it goes in. Flush the wound at once, and never let a held man stay held.

sections.title: Parley (never)
sections.body: I tried, and I tried properly: honey, smoke, a dead hare laid across the path, the courteous forms in three tongues. A soldier walked over the hare to get at me. There is no one home behind those eyes — only the hive, and the hive does not treat.

It notices opponents within 30 feet by scent — 60 feet if upwind, 15 feet if downwind — and doubles or triples those ranges for strong or overpowering smells. The queen is bigger and stronger than any soldier but carries no acid sting, and what treasure a hive holds lies in her chamber.

lore.summary: Centipedes come in every size the dark will allow, from a thing that fits inside a boot to a horror that fills a hall. They are all the same creature grown larger: many legs, a flat body that folds into any crevice, and a pair of venomed fangs behind the head. They hunt underground, climb anything at all, and hide far better than a thing that long has any right to.

sections.title: Hunter's assessment
sections.body:
Size: The kind runs from smaller than a cat to longer than a river barge; the ones a hunter meets most are about the length of a horse.
Durability: Lightly built for all that length — shell over a soft body. They die more readily than they look.
Defenses: Stillness and colouring. Flat against rock they are near invisible until they move, and they see well in the dark; the greatest of them carry shell thick enough to turn a poor blow.
Speed: Quick, and they run up walls and across ceilings at the same pace they cross the floor.
Might: One bite and the venom in it. The larger the centipede the worse both grow; the great ones can take a man in half.
Mind: None. They bite whatever smells of food, and would bite the boot as readily as the foot inside it.
Disposition: Ambushers, not stalkers. They lie folded in a crack and take whatever passes.
Bane: The venom steals your quickness rather than your strength, so a bitten man still swings hard — only slowly. And they are brittle: one honest stroke usually finishes it. Fight with your back to stone where nothing can drop on you.

sections.title: How it fights
sections.body: It waits pressed flat in a crevice or hanging above the passage, then drops or darts and bites. That is the whole of its craft: bite, back off, come again from another angle. The venom does its work across the length of the fight until a man is slow and clumsy and easy to bite once more. The small kinds come in colonies and rely on numbers; the great ones hunt alone and have no need of them.

sections.title: Margin notes
sections.body:
• The venom takes your quickness, not your strength. Fight in a corner and swing straight.
• Look up in a low passage. They hang above the path and drop on the second man in the line.
• They are not tough. One good stroke usually ends it — the trick is finding it before it finds you.

sections.title: Parley (never)
sections.body: I have met these from ankle-height to house-height and never got so much as a pause from one. No ears, and nothing to hear with them. The only conversation on offer is the one you have with your bootheel, or with a spear, depending on the size of it.

sections.body:
Poison (Ex): A monstrous centipede has a poisonous bite. The save DCs are Constitution-based, and the listed damage is both initial and secondary damage. By size: Tiny, Fortitude DC 10, 1 Dex; Small, DC 10, 1d2 Dex; Medium, DC 10, 1d3 Dex; Large, DC 11, 1d4 Dex; Huge, DC 14, 1d6 Dex; Gargantuan, DC 17, 1d8 Dex; Colossal, DC 23, 2d6 Dex. A Large centipede's bite therefore calls for a DC 11 Fortitude save against 1d4 Dexterity, twice over.

Vermin Traits (Ex): Mindless: no Intelligence score, and immunity to all mind-affecting effects (charms, compulsions, phantasms, patterns, and morale effects). Darkvision out to 60 feet. Proficient with their natural weapons only, and with no armour. Vermin breathe, eat, and sleep.

The Kind, Tiny to Colossal: Monstrous centipedes attack anything that resembles food, biting with their jaws and injecting their poison. All are always neutral, carry no treasure, and share darkvision 60 ft. and vermin traits. TINY (CR 1/8): Init +2; Speed 20 ft., climb 20 ft.; AC 14 (+2 size, +2 Dex), touch 14, flat-footed 12; Base Atk/Grp +0/–13; Bite +4 melee (1d3–5 plus poison); Space/Reach 2½ ft./0 ft.; Fort +2, Ref +2, Will +0; Str 1, Dex 15, Con 10, Int —, Wis 10, Cha 2; Climb +10, Hide +18, Spot +4; Weapon Finesse (bonus); colony (8–16). SMALL (CR 1/4): Init +2; Speed 30 ft., climb 30 ft.; AC 14 (+1 size, +2 Dex, +1 natural), touch 13, flat-footed 12; Base Atk/Grp +0/–7; Bite +3 melee (1d4–3 plus poison); Space/Reach 5 ft./5 ft.; Fort +2, Ref +2, Will +0; Str 5, Dex 15, Con 10, Int —, Wis 10, Cha 2; Climb +10, Hide +14, Spot +4; Weapon Finesse (bonus); colony (2–5) or swarm (6–11). MEDIUM (CR 1/2): Init +2; Speed 40 ft., climb 40 ft.; AC 14 (+2 Dex, +2 natural), touch 12, flat-footed 12; Base Atk/Grp +0/–1; Bite +2 melee (1d6–1 plus poison); Space/Reach 5 ft./5 ft.; Fort +2, Ref +2, Will +0; Str 9, Dex 15, Con 10, Int —, Wis 10, Cha 2; Climb +10, Hide +10, Spot +4; Weapon Finesse (bonus); solitary or colony (2–5). LARGE (CR 1) is the reference column above. HUGE (CR 2): Init +2; Speed 40 ft., climb 40 ft.; AC 16 (–2 size, +2 Dex, +6 natural), touch 10, flat-footed 14; Base Atk/Grp +4/+15; Bite +5 melee (2d6+4 plus poison); Space/Reach 15 ft./10 ft.; Fort +6, Ref +4, Will +2; Str 17, Dex 15, Con 12, Int —, Wis 10, Cha 2; Climb +11, Hide +2, Spot +4; no feats; solitary or colony (2–5); Advancement 7–11 levels. GARGANTUAN (CR 6): Init +2; Speed 40 ft., climb 40 ft.; AC 18 (–4 size, +2 Dex, +10 natural), touch 8, flat-footed 16; Base Atk/Grp +9/+27; Bite +11 melee (2d8+9 plus poison); Space/Reach 20 ft./15 ft.; Fort +9, Ref +6, Will +4; Str 23, Dex 15, Con 12, Int —, Wis 10, Cha 2; Climb +14, Hide –2, Spot +4; solitary; Advancement 13–23 levels. COLOSSAL (CR 9): Init +1; Speed 40 ft., climb 40 ft.; AC 20 (–8 size, +2 Dex, +16 natural), touch 4, flat-footed 18; Base Atk/Grp +18/+42; Bite +18 melee (4d6+12 plus poison); Space/Reach 30 ft./20 ft.; Fort +15, Ref +9, Will +8; Str 27, Dex 13, Con 12, Int —, Wis 10, Cha 2; Climb +16, Hide –7, Spot +4; solitary; Advancement 25–48 levels.

lore.summary: Armoured, patient and utterly without thought, the monstrous scorpion is the warm desert's own trap. They come in every stature, from a thing that would sit in your boot to a horror that shades a whole caravan, and all of them are built to one pattern: shears before, venom above, and dark plate over the whole, warm from the sand it lay under.

sections.title: Hunter's assessment
sections.body:
Size: Large, in the size you will most often meet — long as a plough horse and lower to the ground; but the kind runs from vermin you could tread on up to beasts that could take a wagon in one shear.
Durability: Plated from claw to sting; it takes hard, repeated work to break one open.
Defenses: Armour and nothing else — no craft, no magic, no guile. It sees in full dark, and it feels every footfall through the sand, so it is never crept up upon.
Speed: Alarmingly swift over open ground for so heavy a thing, and it climbs rock and wall without slowing.
Might: Two shears that seize and then crush what they hold, and a tail that stoops over its own back to drive the sting home again and again. The venom sickens the blood and wastes the vigour out of a body until the victim cannot stand.
Mind: None at all. It cannot be frightened, charmed, deceived or reasoned with, and no mind-craft, sleep or terror touches it.
Disposition: It charges anything that comes near, whether it means to eat it or not, and it does not break off.
Bane: It has no wits whatever. Bait it with a goat and walk it into your pit; it will take the bait every time. In the open it must come to you, and a braced spear meets it before the shears close.

sections.title: How it fights
sections.body: It charges without warning. It takes hold with a shear, hauls you in against the plates and crushes while the tail comes over the back to sting, and sting again — each strike leaving you weaker than the last. It felt you long before you saw it, so there is no surprising it, and it will not withdraw while anything living still stands in front of it.

sections.title: Margin notes
sections.body:
• Bait it with meat and dig your pit. It has no wits to smell a trap.
• Cut the arms, not the back. The back is where all the armour went.
• Watch the sand, not the beast. It knew my step long before I knew its burrow.

sections.title: Parley (never)
sections.body: Never. There is nobody behind those eyes to answer. I tried it once in three tongues with a goat for a gift; it took the goat and then came for me. Talk instead to the herders who share its ground — they know every burrow on the flat and will sell you the map for a cup of wine.

sections.title: Threat
sections.body: Minor — A minor foe — grown great, a grave one

sections.title: Stat block (SRD)
sections.body:
Size/Type: Large Vermin
Initiative: +0
Speed: 50 ft. (10 squares)
Armor Class: 16 (-1 size, +7 natural), touch 9, flat-footed 16
Base Attack/Grapple: +3/+11
Attack: Claw +6 melee (1d6+4)
Full Attack: 2 claws +6 melee (1d6+4) and sting +1 melee (1d6+2 plus poison)
Space/Reach: 10 ft./5 ft.
Special Attacks: Constrict 1d6+4, improved grab, poison
Special Qualities: Darkvision 60 ft., tremorsense 60 ft., vermin traits
Saves: Fort +6, Ref +1, Will +1
Abilities: Str 19, Dex 10, Con 14, Int —, Wis 10, Cha 2
Skills: Climb +8, Hide +0, Spot +4
Feats: —
Environment: Warm deserts
Organization: Solitary or colony (2-5)
Challenge Rating: 3
Alignment: Always neutral
Treasure: 1/10 coins; 50% goods; 50% items
Advancement: 6-9 levels (Large)

sections.title: Special abilities
sections.body:
Improved Grab (Ex): To use this ability, a monstrous scorpion must hit with a claw attack. It can then attempt to start a grapple as a free action without provoking an attack of opportunity. A monstrous scorpion may use either its Strength modifier or its Dexterity modifier for grapple checks, whichever is better.

Constrict (Ex): A monstrous scorpion deals automatic claw damage on a successful grapple check — 1d6+4 for a Large specimen. Once a claw closes, the pincer keeps crushing every round without the scorpion needing to strike again, which is what makes the sting so hard to avoid.

Poison (Ex): A monstrous scorpion has a poisonous sting. The details vary by the scorpion's size. The save DCs are Constitution-based, and the listed damage is both initial and secondary. Tiny, Fort DC 12, 1 Con; Small, Fort DC 12, 1d2 Con; Medium, Fort DC 13, 1d3 Con; Large, Fort DC 14, 1d4 Con; Huge, Fort DC 18, 1d6 Con; Gargantuan, Fort DC 23, 1d8 Con; Colossal, Fort DC 33, 1d10 Con.

Tremorsense (Ex): A monstrous scorpion automatically senses the location of anything in contact with the ground within 60 feet. Standing still, hiding, or dousing a light does nothing; only leaving the ground does.

Scorpions by Size: The family runs from cat-sized to ship-sized, and every member has the same three tools — two grabbing claws, a poisoned sting, and tremorsense. Tiny: AC 14, 2 claws +2 melee (1d2-4) and sting -3 melee, constrict 1d2-4, Str 3, CR 1/4, colonies of 8-16. Small: AC 14, 2 claws +1 melee (1d3-1) and sting -4 melee, constrict 1d3-1, Str 9, CR 1/2. Medium: AC 14, 2 claws +2 melee (1d4+1) and sting -3 melee, constrict 1d4+1, Str 13, CR 1. Large: AC 16, 2 claws +6 melee (1d6+4) and sting +1 melee, constrict 1d6+4, Str 19, CR 3 — the reference column above. Huge: AC 20, 2 claws +11 melee (1d8+6) and sting +6 melee (2d4+3), constrict 1d8+6, Str 23, 15 ft./10 ft., CR 7. Gargantuan: AC 24, 2 claws +21 melee (2d6+10) and sting +16 melee (2d6+5), constrict 2d6+10, Str 31, 20 ft./15 ft., CR 10. Colossal: AC 26, 2 claws +34 melee (2d8+12) and sting +29 melee (2d8+6), constrict 2d8+12, Str 35, 40 ft./30 ft., CR 12. Speed is 20 ft. for a Tiny scorpion, 30 ft. for a Small, 40 ft. for a Medium, and 50 ft. for every size from Large upward. All sizes are warm-desert dwellers with darkvision 60 ft. and tremorsense 60 ft.

Skills: A monstrous scorpion has a +4 racial bonus on Climb, Hide, and Spot checks.

Vermin Traits: Mindless: no Intelligence score at all, and immunity to every mind-affecting effect (charms, compulsions, phantasms, patterns, and morale effects). Darkvision out to 60 feet. Proficient with its natural weapons only, and with no armor. Vermin breathe, eat, and sleep.

lore.summary: A crop-eater as long as a farm cart, black-shelled and blunt, with jaws like a pair of antlers that close in the middle. One will strip a field in a night; a cluster of them will strip the farm. They breed in temperate woodland and come down to the corn at harvest, and they will walk straight over a man without ever noticing he was there.

sections.title: Hunter's assessment
sections.body:
Size: Large — a beetle the length of a wagon, standing about to a tall man's waist.
Durability: Heavily built and thickly shelled; it soaks up blows that would finish a horse.
Defenses: Nothing but shell and bulk. It sees well in the dark and has no other guard at all.
Speed: Slow. It plods, it never hurries, and — whatever the alehouse says — it does not fly.
Might: The jaws are its whole armoury and they are enough; they close like shears and take a limb off at the joint. Failing that it simply walks over you, and the weight does the rest.
Mind: Mindless, as all vermin are. Nothing you say, show or threaten will turn it from the row it is eating.
Disposition: No hunter of men. It wants the crop, and kills whatever stands between itself and the crop.
Bane: Slow, earthbound and stupid. Stay mounted or get on a wall and it can do nothing to you; then take it from the flank while it feeds. Fire through dry stubble undoes a whole cluster at once.

sections.title: How it fights
sections.body: It goes forward and keeps going forward. If you stand in its road it seizes you in the mandibles and shears; if you fall it tramples, and the weight does more harm than the jaws ever did. It does not manoeuvre, does not flank and does not retreat, and unless you strike it, it will keep eating while you shout.

sections.title: Margin notes
sections.body:
• It cannot fly. Whatever the alewife swore to you. Get high and it is only a slow black rock.
• Take the jaws off with an axe if you get the chance. A beetle that cannot shear is a nuisance, not a danger.
• Cluster means more behind the hedge. Count the shells before you commit.

sections.title: Parley (never)
sections.body: Never — there is nothing there to hear you. But do not kill them wastefully either. A farmer came at me with a bill hook for slaying the cluster in his west field: the shells roofed his barn and the grubs fattened his pigs. Learn what the village wants before you draw.

sections.title: Threat
sections.body: Formidable — A formidable pest

sections.title: Stat block (SRD)
sections.body:
Size/Type: Large Vermin
Initiative: +0
Speed: 20 ft. (4 squares)
Armor Class: 19 (-1 size, +10 natural), touch 9, flat-footed 19
Base Attack/Grapple: +5/+15
Attack: Bite +10 melee (4d6+9)
Full Attack: Bite +10 melee (4d6+9)
Space/Reach: 10 ft./5 ft.
Special Attacks: Trample 2d8+3
Special Qualities: Darkvision 60 ft., vermin traits
Saves: Fort +8, Ref +2, Will +2
Abilities: Str 23, Dex 10, Con 17, Int —, Wis 10, Cha 9
Skills: —
Feats: —
Environment: Temperate forests
Organization: Cluster (2-5) or mass (6-11)
Challenge Rating: 4
Alignment: Always neutral
Treasure: None
Advancement: 8-10 levels (Large); 11-21 levels (Huge)

sections.title: Special abilities
sections.body:
Trample (Ex): As a full-round action, a giant stag beetle can move up to twice its speed and run straight over any opponent at least one size category smaller than itself, dealing 2d8+3 points of bludgeoning damage. It merely has to move over the opponent; any creature whose space is completely covered by the beetle's space is trampled. Trampled opponents may attempt an attack of opportunity at a -4 penalty, or forgo it and attempt a Reflex save (DC 19, Strength-based) for half damage. If the beetle crosses only part of a larger target's space, that target gets the attack of opportunity but is not trampled.

Vermin Traits: Mindless: no Intelligence score at all, and immunity to every mind-affecting effect (charms, compulsions, phantasms, patterns, and morale effects). Darkvision out to 60 feet. Proficient with its natural weapons only, and with no armor. Vermin breathe, eat, and sleep.

lore.summary: A hunting wasp grown as long as a pony, black and amber and light as a kite, working the temperate woods on the wing. It stings until the thing stops moving, then carries the body home and lays its brood in the meat. Met alone it is a hard afternoon; met near the nest, a score of them come off the comb at once.

sections.title: Hunter's assessment
sections.body:
Size: Large — long as a pony but almost nothing in weight, all wing, waist and sting.
Durability: Thin-shelled and brittle for its size. A single good blow tells; two finish it.
Defenses: None worth the name. Its armour is the air — it is simply not where your blade went.
Speed: Plodding and clumsy afoot; swift and beautifully handled aloft, and it never loses its bearings, however far it ranges from the nest.
Might: One sting, driven with the whole body behind it, and the venom takes the nimbleness out of you — the limbs go slack and clumsy, and a second sting atop the first leaves a man unable to lift his own arms.
Mind: Mindless. It stings what is warm, moving and near, and it knows nothing else.
Disposition: It attacks when hungry or when the nest is threatened. Otherwise it will pass overhead about its business and let you be.
Bane: Frail. Reach it and it breaks. Since it must come to you to sting, wait the dive out behind a braced polearm, or throw a net — grounded and tangled, it is already finished.

sections.title: How it fights
sections.body: It hunts on the wing: stoops, stings, and is climbing away before you can answer. The venom does not kill so much as unstring you, and it is patient — it will circle and stoop and circle again until you cannot hold a weapon, and then it carries you home. Near a nest they do not take turns; they all come at once.

sections.title: Margin notes
sections.body:
• The venom does not freeze you outright, whatever the ballads say — it unstrings your limbs by degrees. You can still run. Run early.
• Fight it grounded or not at all. A long spear butted into the earth is worth two swords.
• Search the comb before you fire the nest. They store their meat still breathing.

sections.title: Parley (never)
sections.body: Never; nobody is home behind those eyes. But the nest is worth the walk. Twice I have cut a living man out of the comb — stiff, slack-limbed, laid up as larder and still breathing. Open the cells before you put a torch to it, or you burn somebody's son.

sections.title: Threat
sections.body: Minor — A minor foe, taken singly

sections.title: Stat block (SRD)
sections.body:
Size/Type: Large Vermin
Initiative: +1
Speed: 20 ft. (4 squares), fly 60 ft. (good)
Armor Class: 14 (-1 size, +1 Dex, +4 natural), touch 10, flat-footed 13
Base Attack/Grapple: +3/+11
Attack: Sting +6 melee (1d3+6 plus poison)
Full Attack: Sting +6 melee (1d3+6 plus poison)
Space/Reach: 10 ft./5 ft.
Special Attacks: Poison
Special Qualities: Darkvision 60 ft., vermin traits
Saves: Fort +6, Ref +2, Will +2
Abilities: Str 18, Dex 12, Con 14, Int —, Wis 13, Cha 11
Skills: Spot +9, Survival +1*
Feats: —
Environment: Temperate forests
Organization: Solitary, swarm (2-5), or nest (11-20)
Challenge Rating: 3
Alignment: Always neutral
Treasure: None
Advancement: 6-8 levels (Large); 9-15 levels (Huge)

sections.title: Special abilities
sections.body:
Poison (Ex): Injury, Fortitude DC 14, initial and secondary damage 1d6 Dex. The save DC is Constitution-based. The venom does not kill; it takes the legs out from under the victim, which is exactly what the wasp wants — dead or helpless prey is carried back to the nest as food for the unhatched young.

Skills: Giant wasps have a +8 racial bonus on Spot checks. *They also have a +4 racial bonus on Survival checks to orient themselves, which is how a foraging wasp always finds its way back to the nest.

Vermin Traits: Mindless: no Intelligence score at all, and immunity to every mind-affecting effect (charms, compulsions, phantasms, patterns, and morale effects). Darkvision out to 60 feet. Proficient with its natural weapons only, and with no armor. Vermin breathe, eat, and sleep.

lore.summary: A bat cut out of the substance of night, its spread wings wide enough to roof a cottage, so black that you never see it coming — you notice stars going out in a line. Least of the three nightshades, younger kin to the man-shaped walker that is their middle sibling, it hunts the high dark and eats the enchantment out of your gear before it starts on you.

sections.title: Hunter's assessment
sections.body:
Size: Huge — a bat whose wings would cover a cottage roof, and heavier than it has any right to be.
Durability: Grievously hard to put down. It is dead already, and wounds that would end a living thing barely check it.
Defenses: Silver, or a blessed and enchanted edge, or nothing — honest steel slides off it. Cold does not touch it, and spells slip aside from it more often than they land. Being what it is, it has no fear of poison, sickness, sleep, terror or charm, and a thrust to a vital place means nothing in a body with no vitals.
Speed: Awkward and slow on the ground; on the wing, swift and marvellously handled. It strikes as it passes and is gone before you turn.
Might: Its bite is worse for your gear than your body. The virtue goes out of an enchanted blade or harness a little at every touch, until your grandfather's sword is merely good steel and nothing more. Beyond that it commands smothering darkness, killing cold, a word that stops the heart, and it can call shadows and worse up out of the ground to serve it an hour at a time.
Mind: Sharp, patient and deeply read in magic, and evil clean through. It understands every tongue written or spoken and answers straight into your skull without opening its mouth.
Disposition: A hunter, and a careful one. It prefers the dark and the high air, and will not close until it has thinned and divided you.
Bane: True daylight — the sun's own, not a conjured glow — makes it clumsy at everything it attempts. Silver bites where steel will not. And the ground is not its element: bring it down and it is halved.

sections.title: How it fights
sections.body: It comes out of a black sky in a stoop, bites in passing and climbs away, over and over, never standing to trade blows. Before that it will have drowned the ground in a deeper darkness, quickened itself, and thrown confusion or a holding spell at whoever looked most dangerous. Pressed, it calls shadows up to swarm you while it circles out of reach. Every touch of its jaws leaves your steel a little more ordinary.

sections.title: Margin notes
sections.body:
• Carry silver, and carry a second blade. It drinks the virtue out of an enchanted one a bite at a time.
• Hold out until sunrise if you can. True daylight makes it clumsy; a conjured light does nothing whatever.
• It blots the stars before it blots anything else. Set a watch whose only task is to look up.

sections.title: Parley (never)
sections.body: Never — and I say so knowing full well it will talk. It speaks into your head, courteously, in your mother's voice if it cares to. These things are made of darkness and malice in equal measure; there is no bargain inside them, only delay while the shadows gather. Answer it with silver.

sections.title: Threat
sections.body: Dire — A dire quarry

sections.title: Stat block (SRD)
sections.body:
Size/Type: Huge Undead (Extraplanar)
Initiative: +8
Speed: 20 ft. (4 squares), fly 60 ft. (good)
Armor Class: 30 (-2 size, +4 Dex, +18 natural), touch 12, flat-footed 26
Base Attack/Grapple: +8/+28
Attack: Bite +18 melee (2d6+17/19-20 plus magic drain)
Full Attack: Bite +18 melee (2d6+17/19-20 plus magic drain)
Space/Reach: 15 ft./10 ft.
Special Attacks: Desecrating aura, magic drain, spell-like abilities, summon undead
Special Qualities: Aversion to daylight, damage reduction 15/silver and magic, darkvision 60 ft., immunity to cold, spell resistance 27, telepathy 100 ft., undead traits
Saves: Fort +9, Ref +11, Will +17
Abilities: Str 31, Dex 18, Con —, Int 18, Wis 20, Cha 18
Skills: Concentration +24, Diplomacy +6, Hide +16*, Listen +25, Move Silently +24, Search +24, Sense Motive +25, Spellcraft +24, Spot +25, Survival +5 (+7 following tracks)
Feats: Combat Reflexes, Dodge, Flyby Attack, Great Fortitude, Improved Critical (bite), Improved Initiative
Environment: Plane of Shadow
Organization: Solitary, pair, or flock (3-6)
Challenge Rating: 14
Alignment: Always chaotic evil
Treasure: Standard
Advancement: 18-25 levels (Huge); 26-34 levels (Gargantuan)

sections.title: Special abilities
sections.body:
Magic Drain (Su): A nightwing can weaken magic armor, weapons, and shields by making a successful touch attack. The targeted item must succeed on a DC 22 Fortitude save or lose 1 point of its enhancement bonus; the save DC is Charisma-based. An item stripped of its entire enhancement bonus becomes merely a masterwork item and loses any special abilities (such as flaming) along with it. Casting dispel evil on the item reverses the drain, provided it is done within a number of days after the attack equal to the caster's level and the caster succeeds on a DC 29 caster level check. This is why a party that fights a nightwing and survives often walks away poorer than it walked in.

Spell-Like Abilities: At will—contagion (DC 18), deeper darkness, detect magic, haste, see invisibility, unholy blight (DC 18); 3/day—confusion (DC 18), greater dispel magic, hold monster (DC 19), invisibility; 1/day—cone of cold (DC 19), finger of death (DC 21), plane shift (DC 21). Caster level 17th. The save DCs are Charisma-based.

Summon Undead (Su): A nightwing can summon undead creatures once per night: 5-12 shadows, 2-4 greater shadows, or 1 dread wraith. The summoned undead arrive in 1d10 rounds and serve for 1 hour or until released.

Desecrating Aura (Su): All nightshades give off a 20-foot-radius emanation of utter desecration, soaking their surroundings in negative energy. It works much like a desecrate spell, except that the nightshade's evil is so great that the area counts as the shrine of an evil power. Every undead creature within 20 feet — the nightshade included — gains a +2 profane bonus on attack rolls, damage rolls, and saving throws, and is made proportionally tougher and harder to put down. (The nightshade's attack and save entries given here already include these profane bonuses.) Charisma checks made to turn undead inside the area take a -6 penalty. The aura cannot be dispelled except by dispel evil or a similar effect; if it is dispelled the nightshade can resume it as a free action on its next turn. The aura is suppressed while the nightshade stands in a consecrated or hallowed area, but its presence equally suppresses the consecration or hallowing for as long as it remains.

Aversion to Daylight (Ex): If exposed to natural daylight — not merely a daylight spell — a nightshade takes a -4 penalty on all attack rolls, saving throws, and skill checks.

Telepathy (Su): Nightshades can read and understand every form of communication, but they speak to others only by telepathy, out to 100 feet.

Natural Weapons (Ex): A nightwing's natural weapons count as magic weapons for the purpose of overcoming damage reduction. Its own damage reduction 15/silver and magic means anything less than a silvered or enchanted blade barely scratches it, and it is wholly immune to cold.

Skills: *When hiding in a dark area or flying against a dark sky, a nightwing gains a +8 racial bonus on Hide checks. A nightwing on the wing is all but invisible; watchers notice it only as a moving hole in the stars.

Undead Traits: A nightshade has no Constitution score and is immune to all mind-affecting effects (charms, compulsions, phantasms, patterns, and morale effects), and to poison, sleep effects, paralysis, stunning, disease, and death effects. It is not subject to critical hits, nonlethal damage, ability drain, or energy drain, and is immune to damage to Strength, Dexterity, and Constitution, as well as to fatigue and exhaustion. It is immune to any effect requiring a Fortitude save unless that effect also works on objects or is harmless, and it uses its Charisma modifier for Concentration checks. It is destroyed outright once it has taken enough damage, rather than first falling unconscious, and it is never at risk of destruction from a single massive blow. Negative energy heals it; positive energy harms it. It is unaffected by raise dead and reincarnate, and resurrection works only if it is willing to return. Darkvision 60 feet. It can still be turned or rebuked as undead, but its own desecrating aura imposes a -6 penalty on the attempt, so in practice a cleric standing close enough to matter is fighting uphill.

lore.summary: Greatest and worst of the nightshades: a worm of living blackness, long as a village street and thick as an oak is round, swimming through packed earth as a pike swims through weed. The man-shaped walker is its middle sibling and the winged one the least of the three. It comes up beneath the floor and takes whatever was standing there down with it.

sections.title: Hunter's assessment
sections.body:
Size: Gargantuan — longer than most bridges, and thick enough that its bite takes horse and rider together.
Durability: As near unkillable as anything I have stood before. Already dead, and vast with it.
Defenses: Silver or an enchanted edge, else your weapon may as well be a walking stick. Cold cannot harm it, magic slides off it, and being undead it is proof against poison, disease, terror, sleep, charm and every thrust aimed at a vital place.
Speed: Unhurried above ground; through solid earth it travels faster than a man runs, and it feels every step taken on the surface above it.
Might: A maw that swallows a mounted man whole and a stinging tail whose venom wastes the strength out of the limbs. What it takes down its throat it drinks the life from in the dark while it keeps travelling. It commands frost, madness, holding-spells and a word that kills outright, and it can call shadows and wraiths up to hunt for it while it burrows.
Mind: Brilliant, ancient and thoroughly read, and wholly malign. It speaks mind to mind, and it knows every language that was ever written down.
Disposition: It hunts to unmake. It will strike from below at the strongest of you first, and be gone through the floor before the rest have their blades clear.
Bane: True daylight spoils its aim and its nerve — fight it under an open noon sky if you are given any choice at all. Stand on solid rock or in a boat where it cannot swim to you. And carry a small keen knife on your body, not your belt: swallowed, that knife is the only road out.

sections.title: How it fights
sections.body: It burrows, feels for your footfalls, and erupts under the heaviest-armoured man among you. The bite takes hold, and the next moment you are gone down the throat, where the dark drinks your life away while the gut works on you. The tail stings anything else in reach, sapping the strength from it with every touch. Between bites it throws killing cold and holding spells, calls up wraiths, and drops back into the earth to come again from a quarter you were not watching.

sections.title: Margin notes
sections.body:
• Stone floor, a boat, or bare rock flats. Anywhere it cannot swim up at you from beneath.
• Every man carries a knife on his body, not on his belt. Belts come off inside.
• Daylight lames it. Nightshades keep the dark hours for a reason — make it fight in yours.

sections.title: Parley (never)
sections.body: Never. I have heard one speak — courteous, curious, patient, asking after my companions by name. It had eaten one of them within the hour. Nightshades converse for one purpose only: to keep you standing still. If it addresses you, you are already inside its reach. Move.

sections.title: Threat
sections.body: Legendary — A legendary terror

sections.title: Stat block (SRD)
sections.body:

sections.title: Special abilities
sections.body:
Improved Grab (Ex): To use this ability, a nightcrawler must hit with its bite attack. It can then attempt to start a grapple as a free action without provoking an attack of opportunity. If it wins the grapple check, it establishes a hold and can try to swallow the opponent on the following round.

Swallow Whole (Ex): A nightcrawler can try to swallow a grabbed opponent of Huge size or smaller by making a successful grapple check. Once inside, the victim takes 2d8+12 points of bludgeoning damage plus 12 points of acid damage each round from the gizzard, and is subject to the creature's energy drain at the same time. A swallowed creature can cut its way out with a light slashing or piercing weapon by dealing 35 points of damage to the gizzard (AC 21). Once it climbs out, muscular action closes the hole behind it, so the next swallowed victim must cut its own way out from scratch. A nightcrawler's interior can hold 2 Huge, 8 Large, 32 Medium, 128 Small, or 512 Tiny or smaller opponents.

Energy Drain (Su): Living creatures inside a nightcrawler's gizzard gain one negative level each round. The Fortitude save to remove a negative level is DC 26, and the save DC is Charisma-based. Every negative level it bestows briefly strengthens the nightcrawler, so the longer a victim stays down, the harder the thing above ground becomes to kill.

Poison (Ex): Injury, Fortitude DC 22, initial and secondary damage 2d6 Str. The save DC is Constitution-based. The tail sting is the nightcrawler's second mouth in all but name: it strips the strength out of anyone who survives the bite.

Spell-Like Abilities: At will—contagion (DC 18), deeper darkness, detect magic, greater dispel magic, haste, invisibility, see invisibility, unholy blight (DC 18); 3/day—cone of cold (DC 19), confusion (DC 18), hold monster (DC 19); 1/day—finger of death (DC 21), mass hold monster (DC 23), plane shift (DC 21). Caster level 25th. The save DCs are Charisma-based.

Summon Undead (Su): A nightcrawler can summon undead creatures once per night: 9-16 shadows, 3-6 greater shadows, or 2-4 dread wraiths. The summoned undead arrive in 1d10 rounds and serve for 1 hour or until released.

Desecrating Aura (Su): All nightshades give off a 20-foot-radius emanation of utter desecration, soaking their surroundings in negative energy. It works much like a desecrate spell, except that the nightshade's evil is so great that the area counts as the shrine of an evil power. Every undead creature within 20 feet — the nightshade included — gains a +2 profane bonus on attack rolls, damage rolls, and saving throws, and is made proportionally tougher and harder to put down. (The nightshade's attack and save entries given here already include these profane bonuses.) Charisma checks made to turn undead inside the area take a -6 penalty. The aura cannot be dispelled except by dispel evil or a similar effect; if it is dispelled the nightshade can resume it as a free action on its next turn. The aura is suppressed while the nightshade stands in a consecrated or hallowed area, but its presence equally suppresses the consecration or hallowing for as long as it remains.

Aversion to Daylight (Ex): If exposed to natural daylight — not merely a daylight spell — a nightshade takes a -4 penalty on all attack rolls, saving throws, and skill checks.

Tremorsense (Ex): A nightcrawler automatically senses the location of anything in contact with the ground within 60 feet. It burrows at 60 feet and strikes from below; standing still on open ground hides nothing from it.

Telepathy (Su): Nightshades can read and understand every form of communication, but they speak to others only by telepathy, out to 100 feet.

Natural Weapons (Ex): A nightcrawler's natural weapons count as magic weapons for the purpose of overcoming damage reduction. Its own damage reduction 15/silver and magic and its immunity to cold make ordinary steel and winter magic near-useless against it.

Undead Traits: A nightshade has no Constitution score and is immune to all mind-affecting effects (charms, compulsions, phantasms, patterns, and morale effects), and to poison, sleep effects, paralysis, stunning, disease, and death effects. It is not subject to critical hits, nonlethal damage, ability drain, or energy drain, and is immune to damage to Strength, Dexterity, and Constitution, as well as to fatigue and exhaustion. It is immune to any effect requiring a Fortitude save unless that effect also works on objects or is harmless, and it uses its Charisma modifier for Concentration checks. It is destroyed outright once it has taken enough damage, rather than first falling unconscious, and it is never at risk of destruction from a single massive blow. Negative energy heals it; positive energy harms it. It is unaffected by raise dead and reincarnate, and resurrection works only if it is willing to return. Darkvision 60 feet. It can still be turned or rebuked as undead, but its own desecrating aura imposes a -6 penalty on the attempt, so in practice a cleric standing close enough to matter is fighting uphill.

lore.summary: Mottled grey or black, longer than a rowboat and heavier than a man in full harness, the dire wolf is the temperate forest's verdict on the careless. They run in packs, ringing whatever they have chosen, taking it off its feet, and killing anything they can catch. Where one howls, count the answers before you make camp.

sections.title: Hunter's assessment
sections.body:
Size: Large — longer than a war-horse, and heavier under the fur than it looks.
Durability: Hardy as anything bred by deep woodland; it will run all day and bleed all night.
Defenses: No armour but a thick pelt and a low, quick carriage. Steel marks it well enough, if you can land the stroke.
Speed: Swifter than a horse over broken ground, and tireless on a long trail. You will not outrun it, so do not try.
Might: One appalling bite that closes on a limb and hauls the whole man down with it.
Mind: An animal's wit, but a hunter's — it reads ground, wind and weakness, and it knows which of you is limping.
Disposition: Not malice. Hunger, and a pack that has already chosen which of you it wants.
Bane: Alone it is only a wolf. Break the ring — a stone at your back, a narrow place, high ground — and the pack loses its entire art.

sections.title: How it fights
sections.body: They come from several sides at once and circle, working to catch a man between them and flank him. Each rush is a single crushing bite, aimed low, that hooks behind the knee and puts the fellow flat on his back; the rest are on him before his shield comes up. On your back, in the open, among wolves, is how good men die in the northern woods.

sections.title: Margin notes
sections.body:
• Back to stone or a broad trunk. They win by circling; deny them the circle.
• They knock you flat first and eat second. A braced spear serves better than your good sword.
• Bleed a carcass upwind and go the other way. Cheaper than a fight, and honest work.

sections.title: Parley (never)
sections.body: Never. I have tried — I have spoken with far worse and been heard. A dire wolf has the wit of a good hound and none of a hound's debts to men. The once a pack let me walk off, it was because I had left them a deer, not because I had left them words.

sections.title: Special abilities

Combat: Dire wolves prefer to attack in packs, surrounding and flanking a foe when they can. They are efficient pack hunters that will kill anything they can catch.

Trip (Ex): A dire wolf that hits with a bite attack can attempt to trip its opponent (+11 check modifier) as a free action without making a touch attack or provoking an attack of opportunity. If the attempt fails, the opponent cannot react to trip the dire wolf.

Scent (Ex): A dire wolf can detect approaching enemies, sniff out hidden foes, and track by sense of smell. It notices creatures by scent within 30 feet (60 feet upwind, 15 feet downwind), and can follow a trail by smell, though it cannot pinpoint a creature's exact location by scent alone.

Skills: A dire wolf has a +2 racial bonus on Hide, Listen, Move Silently, and Spot checks. *It also has a +4 racial bonus on Survival checks when tracking by scent.

lore.summary: The cave bear that never stopped growing: a shaggy hill of a thing, longer than a cart and heavier than a team of draught horses, at home in cold forest. It takes no interest in those who give it room. Come near its kill, its cache or its cubs, however, and it will tear apart anything that might hold something edible — and it does not look closely first.

sections.title: Hunter's assessment
sections.body:
Size: Large, though the word does it no honour — reared up, it puts the trees in shadow.
Durability: Immense. Wounds that would settle a bull merely make it louder.
Defenses: A pelt like packed felt over gristle and heavy bone; blades go in shallow and come out hard.
Speed: Faster than anything that heavy has a right to be, over ground and through water alike.
Might: Two raking forepaws and a bite behind them. The paws are the true danger — once they close, you are held, and the rest is done at leisure.
Mind: Beast-wit, with a long memory for where food was last found.
Disposition: Placid, even indifferent, until you come at its food. Then nothing else on the mountain matters to it.
Bane: It has no reach past its own arms and no answer to height. A ledge, a stout branch or open country are all safer than a thicket — and it will let you leave, if leaving is all you do.

sections.title: How it fights
sections.body: It rears, crosses the ground in a rush, and tears with both forepaws. Where a paw lands it seizes, and it drags a man in against its chest to work him over with the other paw and its jaws. It fights standing over whatever it was defending, gives no ground, and will not be driven off by noise the way a lesser bear might.

sections.title: Margin notes
sections.body:
• Walk away from its kill. That is the whole of the treaty, and it holds.
• Once those paws have you, a blade is a poor friend. Carry something to break the hold, or a companion who will.
• Do not run and do not swim. It does both better than you, and downhill it is worse.

sections.title: Parley (never)
sections.body: Never — which is not the same as always fighting. Twice I have backed away from one with my hands open and my eyes down, and twice it let me go. It cannot be reasoned with. It can be conceded to. Leave the carcass. It was never yours.

lore.summary: A hog swollen to the bulk of an ox, all shoulder and tusk, rooting through temperate woodland with its herd about it. It eats whatever it finds and attacks whatever comes near, without provocation and without pause. Many a hunter has been opened up by a boar he was quite certain had already died.

sections.title: Hunter's assessment
sections.body:
Size: Large — mostly shoulder and neck, and every stone of it pointed forwards.
Durability: Layered in fat and muscle. It soaks up punishment that ought to fell a horse and keeps coming.
Defenses: Hide like boiled leather over a wall of gristle; arrows lodge in it and are ignored.
Speed: A short, ruinous burst in a straight line. Poor at turning, and worse in close timber.
Might: Tusks driven by the entire weight of the beast — a charge that opens a man from hip to shoulder.
Mind: Dull, short-tempered and incurious. No cunning whatever, and none required.
Disposition: Foul-tempered over nothing in particular. It charges because you are standing where you are.
Bane: It runs straight and it never learns. Step aside at the last instant, or keep a thick trunk between you, and it must labour round for another pass while you choose where to stand.

sections.title: How it fights
sections.body: It charges, and that is the beginning and most of the middle of it: head down, tusks up, straight through whatever stands before it. If the first pass fails it wheels and comes again. Worst of all, it keeps coming long past the point where any honest animal would lie down — gored through, staggering, still fighting as well as it ever did. Do not drop your guard because it is dying.

sections.title: Margin notes
sections.body:
• Trees. Know where the nearest one is before you ever nock an arrow.
• It fights on well past its dying. Do not turn your back on a fallen boar until it has gone cold.
• Braced spear, butt in the dirt, and let its own charge do the work. Your arms will not.

sections.title: Parley (never)
sections.body: Never. There is nothing behind those small eyes to bargain with — a bad-tempered pig, made enormous. The only words that ever served me against one were the ones I bellowed at my companions to get themselves behind the trees.

Combat: A dire boar charges its opponent, trying to rip the target open with its tusks. Dire boars spend most of their time rooting around as ordinary pigs do, but viciously attack anything that approaches them.

Ferocity (Ex): A dire boar is such a tenacious combatant that it continues to fight without penalty even while disabled or dying — it fights on even when mortally wounded, and only death stops it.

Scent (Ex): A dire boar can detect approaching enemies, sniff out hidden foes, and track by sense of smell. It notices creatures by scent within 30 feet (60 feet upwind, 15 feet downwind), and can follow a trail by smell, though it cannot pinpoint a creature's exact location by scent alone.

lore.summary: The great cat of the warm plains, grown longer than a wagon and heavier than a war-horse. Patient as its lesser cousins and a good deal bolder, it takes prey far above its own weight. It hunts alone, in pairs, or in a pride that works the tall grass like a drawn net — and you will not see it until it is already in the air.

sections.title: Hunter's assessment
sections.body:
Size: Large — longer than a wagon, and it moves as though it were half the weight.
Durability: Solidly built; no single fine stroke will end it.
Defenses: Hide and hair only. But tall grass hides it better than any mail hides you.
Speed: Fast across open plain, and it covers the last of the distance in leaps rather than strides.
Might: Two raking forepaws and jaws that take hold. Once it has borne you down it works with all four sets of claws at once.
Mind: Beast-wit, but a patient one. It will watch a camp a long while and choose the sentry who yawns.
Disposition: A hunter and nothing more. It weighs you as meat and picks the easiest of you.
Bane: Its whole craft is the first leap. Be seen, be loud, be facing it — a cat robbed of surprise will often decide you are not worth the trouble and drift back into the grass.

sections.title: How it fights
sections.body: It stalks flat through cover, then charges and leaps, arriving with both forepaws and its jaws in one motion. If the jaws take hold you are borne down and raked with its hind claws while it holds you — all the killing happens on the ground. It favours whoever walks at the edge of a party, and it will spring at creatures considerably larger than itself without hesitating.

sections.title: Margin notes
sections.body:
• Watch the grass, not the horizon. It comes flat, and it comes very fast.
• Never walk last and never walk alone. It takes the straggler, every time.
• Once it has you down, its hind feet are the killer. Get out from under it before you worry about your sword.

sections.title: Parley (never)
sections.body: Never. It is a cat, and cats do not negotiate; they merely reconsider. I have turned two aside by making myself large and shouting until my throat tore, which is as near to conversation as the plains permit.

sections.title: Special abilities
sections.body:
Combat: A dire lion attacks by running at prey, leaping, and clawing and biting as it rakes with its rear claws. It often jumps onto a creature larger than itself. Dire lions are patient hunters, just like their smaller cousins, but apt to take on bigger prey.

Improved Grab (Ex): To use this ability, a dire lion must hit with its bite attack. It can then attempt to start a grapple as a free action without provoking an attack of opportunity. If it wins the grapple check, it establishes a hold and can rake.

Pounce (Ex): If a dire lion charges, it can make a full attack, including two rake attacks.

Rake (Ex): Attack bonus +12 melee, damage 1d6+3.

Scent (Ex): A dire lion can detect approaching enemies, sniff out hidden foes, and track by sense of smell. It notices creatures by scent within 30 feet (60 feet upwind, 15 feet downwind), and can follow a trail by smell, though it cannot pinpoint a creature's exact location by scent alone.

Skills: Dire lions have a +4 racial bonus on Hide and Move Silently checks. *In areas of tall grass or heavy undergrowth, the Hide bonus improves to +8.

lore.summary: Lord of the warm forests: striped, silent, and heavier than a laden cart, with forepaws broad as a shield boss. It hunts alone or with a mate and preys on anything that moves. It will follow a party for days without once being seen, waiting on the single hour of the night when nobody is watching properly.

sections.title: Hunter's assessment
sections.body:
Size: Large, but with a bulk and a reach beyond anything else that carries the word lightly.
Durability: Enormously tough. It takes a great deal of killing and allows you very little time in which to do it.
Defenses: No armour, only muscle and stripes — and in dappled green the stripes serve it better than plate.
Speed: Fast, and a tremendous leaper. It swims well, so a river is no wall between you.
Might: The most brutal cat that walks — shearing forepaws, jaws that seize, and hind claws that open what those jaws hold.
Mind: An animal, but a patient and calculating one. It studies a camp before it chooses from it.
Disposition: Solitary and utterly certain of itself. It does not test you first, and it does not posture.
Bane: Everything it has is in the ambush. Open ground, ringed fires and a watch that stays awake strip away most of its advantage — and a spring that fails will send it back into the green rather than into a straight fight.

sections.title: How it fights
sections.body: It waits, sometimes for days, then charges out of cover and leaps, striking with both forepaws and its jaws in the same instant. What it bites it holds; what it holds it opens with the hind claws. It chooses the largest of you or the most isolated, and if the first spring fails it withdraws into the green and begins the patient work again.

sections.title: Margin notes
sections.body:
• It follows for days. When the birds go quiet on the fourth evening, you are the hunted.
• Fires in a ring, two sentries facing outward. It takes the sleeper and it takes the loner.
• Get free of the jaws first. While it holds you, its hind feet are opening your belly.

sections.title: Parley (never)
sections.body: Never, and unlike the lion it cannot be shouted down. The one I hunted longest in the Verdant Coil watched my fires for four nights before it moved. There is no talking to a thing that has already settled how you are to die — there is only being awake when it comes.

Improved Grab (Ex): To use this ability, a dire tiger must hit with its bite attack. It can then attempt to start a grapple as a free action without provoking an attack of opportunity. If it wins the grapple check, it establishes a hold and can rake.

lore.summary: Taller than a mounted man and heavier than a plough-ox, the dire ape holds a stretch of warm forest and suffers nothing living to cross it — not woodsman, not deer, not another of its own kind. Look up when you enter its ground. It travels the canopy as easily as you walk the path, and it has been watching you since the treeline.

sections.title: Hunter's assessment
sections.body:
Size: Large — a black-furred giant that stands head and shoulders over a tall man.
Durability: Thickly built and slow to fall; it soaks punishment that would drop a horse.
Defenses: No armour but hide and muscle, and the hide is tougher than it looks.
Speed: Quick enough afoot, quicker still in the branches — it climbs as surely as you stroll.
Might: Terrible. Hooked hands that seize and drag; when both find purchase it tears the flesh from your ribs.
Mind: Beast-dull, yet with a beast's cunning for ambush and a long memory for its own borders.
Disposition: Furious and territorial. It attacks whatever enters its ground, its own kind included.
Bane: It has no answer to distance. Nothing it does reaches past the length of its arms — open ground, a bow, and a horse beat it every time.

sections.title: How it fights
sections.body: It comes straight in, hands first, and trusts its weight to end matters. Should your mail turn the claws it changes tack at once: grapple, drag you down, pin you flat and rend. With both hands upon you the wound is ruinous. It fights over its ground until one of you has stopped moving, and it does not withdraw to think the matter over.

sections.title: Margin notes
sections.body:
• Look up first. Always up. They drop out of the canopy and the fight begins on your back.
• If your armour turns it, expect hands next. A pinned man is a torn man — keep a short blade at the hip.
• Its border is written in snapped branches at shoulder height. Read it, walk around it, live.

sections.title: Parley (never)
sections.body: There is no talking to it. I tried once in the warm forest south of the Vale, hands open and empty, and it read the gesture as a challenge to its border. An ape has no words and no bargain in it — only a line drawn in broken branches. Honour the line or bring a bow.

sections.body: Minor — A lesser peril

sections.body:

sections.title: Special abilities
sections.body:
Combat: Dire apes attack anything that enters their territory, even other dire apes. If an opponent's armor foils a dire ape's attacks, the creature will attempt to grapple and pin, then rend the prone opponent.

Rend (Ex): A dire ape that hits with both claw attacks latches onto the opponent's body and tears the flesh. This attack automatically deals an extra 2d6+9 points of damage.

lore.summary: Long as a hound and twice as bold, the dire rat is the commonest quarry in the world and the one that kills most often — not by tooth but by what rides upon the tooth. They scavenge anything, nest anywhere from cellar to sewer to ship's hold, climb sheer stone and swim better than most men. Where one shows itself, a score are watching.

sections.title: Hunter's assessment
sections.body:
Size: Small — the bulk of a large dog, all wet fur and yellow incisors.
Durability: Frail. A boot heel does for one.
Defenses: None worth the name, though it is nimble and hard to strike in a dark passage.
Speed: Fast on the flat, faster up a wall, and it swims like an otter.
Might: Feeble alone. It is the filth on the bite that does the harm, never the bite itself.
Mind: Dull as any vermin, but fearless — a pack of them will come at armoured men without pause.
Disposition: Scavengers first. They will not stalk a healthy man, yet they defend a nest to the last of them.
Bane: So frail that anything sweeping a wide space ends a whole pack at once. The true danger comes afterwards, in the fever — guard against that and the fight was nothing.

sections.title: How it fights
sections.body: They swarm without fear, biting and chewing with those chisel teeth, and they will climb your legs, drop from beams and follow you into the water. Any single bite is a scratch. A score of bites is a bad evening and a filth fever that comes days later to waste your strength and your wind while you lie abed and curse.

sections.title: Margin notes
sections.body:
• Wash and burn every bite the same night. The fever arrives days later and steals your strength and your breath.
• They climb and they swim. There is no getting above them and no losing them across a stream.
• Where you meet one, the nest is close. Find the nest or you will be fighting them all week.

sections.title: Parley (never)
sections.body: Vermin. I have spoken with far worse and been answered civilly, but never with a rat. They understand the shape of a torch and nothing else. Kill them quickly, burn the nest, then wash the bite — the fever takes from you what the rat could not.

sections.title: Special abilities
sections.body:
Combat: Dire rats are omnivorous scavengers, but will attack to defend their nests and territories. Dire rat packs attack fearlessly, biting and chewing with their sharp incisors.

Disease (Ex): Filth fever - bite, Fortitude DC 11, incubation period 1d3 days, damage 1d3 Dex and 1d3 Con. The save DC is Constitution-based.

Skills: Dire rats have a +8 racial bonus on Swim checks. Dire rats have a +8 racial bonus on Climb checks and can always choose to take 10 on Climb checks, even if rushed or threatened. Dire rats use their Dexterity modifier for Climb and Swim checks.

lore.summary: Low, broad and shaggy as a landslide, the dire wolverine of the cold forests fears nothing that walks. It is a born tracker, nose to the snow, and will hold a trail for days out of what looks very like spite. It climbs when it must. Bears give ground to it and are wise to do so. It attacks what it meets, wantonly, whatever the odds against.

sections.title: Hunter's assessment
sections.body:
Size: Large — long-bodied and low, heavier than a bear though it stands no higher than your chest.
Durability: Immensely tough, and toughest of all once it is hurt.
Defenses: Dense winter fur over heavy hide; not armour, but it turns a glancing stroke.
Speed: Steady rather than swift across snow, and it climbs well enough to fetch you down from a tree.
Might: Hooked claws and a crushing bite together, and in its fury every blow lands harder than the last.
Mind: Animal, but a hunter's mind — it works a scent trail as well as any hound I have kept, and it does not lose one.
Disposition: Wanton. It attacks whatever it meets, unprovoked, and it will not break off.
Bane: Its fury is a rope you may pull. Once bleeding it goes heedless — stronger, but wide open and blind to its own guard, and it will follow you into whatever you have prepared. Blood it, then lead it.

sections.title: How it fights
sections.body: It charges without cause, claws and teeth at once. Wound it and it turns berserk on the instant: mightier, harder to lay out, and utterly careless of its own defence, and it cannot calm again while either of you draws breath. There is no driving one off, no showing it a torch. There is killing it, or there is being somewhere else when it arrives.

sections.title: Margin notes
sections.body:
• Once it bleeds it cannot stop. Fight it over a pit, never over open snow.
• It tracks better than my hounds did. Cross water, and keep crossing.
• Camp downwind and cook nothing. It will come the length of a valley for the smell alone.

sections.title: Parley (never)
sections.body: None. I have made peace with hags and with dragons; I have never made peace with a wolverine. It wants no food of yours, no ground, no surrender. What I offer one now is distance and a cold camp downwind, and that is the only bargain it has ever kept with me.
