sections.title: Special abilities
sections.body:
Combat: These jungle cats are about 4 feet long and weigh about 120 pounds. They usually hunt at night. The statistics presented here can describe any feline of similar size, such as jaguars, panthers, and mountain lions.

Improved Grab (Ex): To use this ability, a leopard must hit with its bite attack. It can then attempt to start a grapple as a free action without provoking an attack of opportunity. If it wins the grapple check, it establishes a hold and can rake.

Pounce (Ex): If a leopard charges a foe, it can make a full attack, including two rake attacks.

Rake (Ex): Attack bonus +6 melee, damage 1d3+1.

Scent (Ex): This ability lets the creature detect approaching enemies, sniff out hidden foes, and track by sense of smell. It can detect opponents within 30 feet by smell; if the opponent is upwind the range increases to 60 feet, and if downwind it drops to 15 feet. Strong scents such as smoke or rotting garbage can be detected at twice those ranges, and overpowering scents at triple. Detecting a scent reveals only that a source is present somewhere within range; the creature can take a move action to note the direction, and it pinpoints the source when it comes within 5 feet of it. A creature with the Track feat and the scent ability can follow tracks by smell, making a Survival check to find or follow a trail — DC 10 for a fresh trail, increased by 2 for each hour the trail is cold, and modified by how strong the quarry's odor is and how many creatures made the trail. Creatures tracking by scent ignore the effects of surface conditions and poor visibility.

Low-Light Vision (Ex): The creature can see twice as far as a human in starlight, moonlight, torchlight, and similar conditions of poor illumination. It retains the ability to distinguish color and detail under these conditions.

Skills: Leopards have a +8 racial bonus on Jump checks and a +4 racial bonus on Hide and Move Silently checks. Leopards have a +8 racial bonus on Balance and Climb checks. A leopard can always choose to take 10 on a Climb check, even if rushed or threatened. *In areas of tall grass or heavy undergrowth, the Hide bonus improves to +8.

lore.summary: Pack hunters of the warm deserts, infamous for their cunning and for the noise they make — a laughing in the dark that is not laughter. Striped, high at the shoulder and sloping away behind, with a jaw out of all proportion to the rest. Gnolls keep them as we keep hounds, and they run a dozen strong and more.

sections.title: Hunter's assessment
sections.body:
Size: Medium — an ill-made dog, high at the shoulder and falling away to the rump.
Durability: Not a great deal. But there is never only one of them.
Defenses: None worth the name: a thick neck, a thicker skull, and numbers.
Speed: Fast and enduring both. It will follow a bleeding man through a day and the night after it.
Might: That jaw is stronger than it has any right to be, and the bite is aimed to take your feet away.
Mind: Cunning — more so than a wolf, to my eye — and it works a flank with real understanding.
Disposition: A scavenger first and a hunter second. It wants the weak, the wounded, and whatever the fire is guarding.
Bane: Craven on its own and easily broken by a determined stand. Drop the bold ones first and the rest lose their nerve.

sections.title: How it fights
sections.body: The pack does what wolves do: a few at the front to hold your eyes while the rest come round to the flanks and the back. The bite goes low, to pull you down. Where gnolls run with them the hyenas take the flanks and the gnoll spears take the front, and I have watched that arrangement work on better men than me.

sections.title: Margin notes
sections.body:
• The laughing starts when they have finished counting. It means you are already circled.
• Guard the wounded man and guard the pack meat. Those are the only things they came for.
• Where hyenas run, gnolls are not far off — or the other way about. Either way, look for spears.

sections.title: Parley (never)
sections.body: Never with the beast — though the gnolls beside it can sometimes be bargained with, and the pack goes wherever the gnolls go. Speak to the master, not the hound. I bought a night's peace off a gnoll hunting party with salt and a bad joke; the hyenas laughed either way.

Combat: Hyenas are pack hunters infamous for their cunning and their unnerving vocalizations. The statistics presented here are for a striped hyena, which is about 3 feet long and weighs about 120 pounds. A favorite tactic is to send a few individuals against the foe's front while the rest of the pack circles and attacks from the flanks or rear.

Trip (Ex): A hyena that hits with its bite attack can attempt to trip the opponent (+2 check modifier) as a free action without making a touch attack or provoking an attack of opportunity. If the attempt fails, the opponent cannot react to trip the hyena.

Strong scents such as smoke or rotting garbage can be detected at twice those ranges, and overpowering scents at triple. Detecting a scent reveals only that a source is present somewhere within range; the creature can take a move action to note the direction, and it pinpoints the source when it comes within 5 feet of it. lore.summary: Not the marsh lizard of the shallows but its elder — a salt-water giant longer than a river barge, lying in the brackish channels of warm marsh with nothing above the surface but two ridged eyes and a pair of nostrils. Where the common crocodile takes goats and dogs, this one takes the boat they were riding in.

sections.title: Hunter's assessment
sections.body:
Size: Huge — longer than a war-canoe and broader than anything else that walks the marsh.
Durability: Enormously tough; it soaks punishment and never loosens its grip while doing so.
Defenses: Ridged plate down back and flank turns a blade aside, it sees well in gloom, and it lies all but invisible with only eyes and nostrils breaking the water.
Speed: Ponderous on land, a terror in the water, and quicker over the first few strides out of the shallows than any man expects.
Might: A bite that folds a shield around the arm behind it, and a tail slap that breaks legs.
Mind: Dull as a stone. It knows hunger, warmth and the edge of its own water, and nothing beyond.
Disposition: Aggressive and patient in equal measure — it waits, mostly submerged, for prey to come within reach, and takes whatever comes.
Bane: It must fight in the water to win. Draw it onto dry ground, or stay off the bank entirely, and its whole craft is gone.

sections.title: How it fights
sections.body: It lies submerged until you are within reach, then comes up all at once and closes its jaws on the nearest limb. What it bites it holds; what it holds it drags into deep water and pins to the bottom until the drowning does its work. Anything it cannot seize it sweeps off its feet with the tail and takes on the second pass.

sections.title: Margin notes
sections.body:
• It fights in the water and loses on land. Fight it where it cannot swim, or do not fight it.
• Carry a bar or a stout haft to lever the jaws. Once it has you, cutting comes far too late.
• Count the eyes on the water before you wade. Where there is one there is often a colony.

sections.title: Parley (never)
sections.body: None. There is nothing behind those eyes to speak to — hunger, warmth, and the edge of its water. I have thrown a slaughtered goat into a channel to buy a crossing; that is not parley, that is paying a toll, and you still cross fast.

sections.title: Special abilities

If it wins the grapple check, the crocodile establishes a hold on the opponent with its mouth and drags it into deep water, attempting to pin it to the bottom.

Common Crocodile: The ordinary crocodile is an aggressive predator 11 to 12 feet long: Medium Animal, Challenge Rating 2, Init +1, Speed 20 ft., swim 30 ft.; AC 15 (+1 Dex, +4 natural), touch 11, flat-footed 14; Base Attack/Grapple +2/+6; bite +6 melee (1d8+6) or tail slap +6 melee (1d12+6); Space/Reach 5 ft./5 ft.; Fort +6, Ref +4, Will +2; Str 19, Dex 12, Con 17, Int 1, Wis 12, Cha 2; Skills Hide +7*, Listen +4, Spot +4, Swim +12; Feats Alertness, Skill Focus (Hide); warm marshes; solitary or colony (6–11); advances to 5 levels (Medium). lore.summary: A serpent thick as a man's waist and longer than a barn, moving through the canopy and the flooded roots of warm forest. The ordinary constrictor is a shy thing that flees when confronted; this one does not. It must eat a great deal to keep that bulk alive, and you are meat enough to be worth its trouble.

sections.title: Hunter's assessment
sections.body:
Size: Huge — a rope of muscle longer than the hall you would fight it in.
Durability: Hardy and stubborn. It does not tire, and it does not let go because it is hurt.
Defenses: No armour worth the name, only tough hide and a long body with no one place worth striking.
Speed: Unhurried across the ground, but it climbs as readily as it crawls and swims as well as it climbs. There is no ground it cannot follow you over.
Might: The bite is the lesser half. The coils crush ribs and stop the breath, and they tighten every time you let one out.
Mind: Dull. It follows scent and warmth to a meal and reckons nothing further.
Disposition: Bolder than its smaller cousin and always hungry. It hunts rather than hides, and it does not trouble with prey too large to coil.
Bane: It stakes everything on one hold. Break the grip, or take the head, and it has no second craft to fall back on.

sections.title: How it fights
sections.body: It comes from a branch overhead or out of the water at your knees, bites to fasten itself, and throws its coils about you in the same motion. Then it simply squeezes and waits. It will not release a hold to strike at your companions — it finishes what it has, which is the one mercy in it, and the reason your companions must be quick.

sections.title: Margin notes
sections.body:
• Work from the tail, not the head. The coils come loose from the far end.
• Look up in warm forest. It hunts from the branches and looks like every other branch.
• A knife on your belt is no use with your arms pinned. Wear one at the wrist.

sections.title: Parley (never)
sections.body: No. I once lay still at arm's length from a great constrictor while it decided what I was, and there was no decision there to appeal to — only a sum of size against size. Be too large to coil, or be somewhere else. Those are the terms it offers.

Improved Grab (Ex): To use this ability, a giant constrictor snake must hit with its bite attack. It can then attempt to start a grapple as a free action without provoking an attack of opportunity. If it wins the grapple check, it establishes a hold and can constrict.

Skills: Snakes have a +4 racial bonus on Hide, Listen, and Spot checks and a +8 racial bonus on Balance and Climb checks. A snake can always choose to take 10 on a Climb check, even if rushed or threatened. Snakes use either their Strength modifier or Dexterity modifier for Climb checks, whichever is higher. A snake has a +8 racial bonus on any Swim check to perform some special action or avoid a hazard. It can always choose to take 10 on a Swim check, even if distracted or endangered. It can use the run action while swimming, provided it swims in a straight line.

Constrictor Snake: The ordinary constrictor snake is a Medium Animal, Challenge Rating 2, Init +7, Speed 20 ft., climb 20 ft., swim 20 ft.; AC 15 (+3 Dex, +2 natural), touch 13, flat-footed 12; Base Attack/Grapple +2/+5; bite +5 melee (1d3+4); Space/Reach 5 ft./5 ft.; Special Attacks constrict 1d3+4, improved grab; Fort +4, Ref +6, Will +2; Str 17, Dex 17, Con 13, Int 1, Wis 12, Cha 2; Skills Balance +11, Climb +14, Hide +10, Listen +7, Spot +7, Swim +11; Feats Alertness, Improved Initiative, Toughness; warm forests; solitary; advances to 5 levels (Medium) or 6–10 levels (Large). Constrictor snakes usually are not aggressive and flee when confronted. They hunt for food but do not attempt to make a meal out of any creature that is too large to constrict. Giant constrictor snakes are more aggressive than their smaller cousins, principally because they need a great amount of food to survive.

lore.summary: The venomous serpents, from a thing that would coil in your palm to a marsh-monster thick as your thigh. All keep the same craft: a hollow-fanged bite that sets a wasting in the blood, robbing a man of his vigour long after the wound has stopped bleeding. Commonest in temperate marsh, and in every dark quiet place a snake may lie.

sections.title: Hunter's assessment
sections.body:
Size: From the least, no longer than your forearm, to the greatest, longer than a horse. The venom is the same at every size — only the reach and the dose change.
Durability: Slight. Even the largest is a thin thing. Fear the poison, not the beast carrying it.
Defenses: Concealment and speed. The small ones are near impossible to see until they have already moved.
Speed: Quick to strike and quicker to leave. It climbs, swims, and balances along a reed as easily as it crosses open ground.
Might: The jaws are nothing. The venom is the weapon — it saps the strength out of a man, and then, when he believes himself past the worst, saps it again.
Mind: Nothing to speak of. Warm from cold, near from far, and no more than that.
Disposition: Not aggressive. It would far rather be gone; it bites when trodden upon or cornered, and then makes off.
Bane: It is fragile and it does not want the fight. Give it room and it leaves. Press it and a staff's length of reach settles the matter before the fangs ever come near you.

sections.title: How it fights
sections.body: It lies hidden until you are close, lashes out with a single bite, and withdraws. It has no interest in pressing an attack it can simply walk away from. The strike itself is seldom the danger — the danger is the hours afterward, when the venom takes hold, and then takes hold a second time.

sections.title: Margin notes
sections.body:
• Boots to the knee and a staff to part the reeds a pace ahead of your feet.
• Bind the limb, keep the man still and low. Running spreads it faster than the snake ever could.
• The wound looks like nothing at all by evening. That is precisely when the second wasting comes.

sections.title: Parley (never)
sections.body: There is nothing to say to a snake. But I will say this for the viper: of every beast in this book it is the least eager to meet you. Walk heavy, sound the reeds ahead, and most of them will be long gone before you knew they were ever there.

lore.summary: An aggressive, territorial hunter of warm seas, with arms longer than a man is tall, each studded with barbs and sharp-edged suckers. It takes the colour of the rock it lies against, and pours its whole bulk through a crack you would not post a letter through. Swimmers do not see it coming. They are simply gone.

sections.title: Hunter's assessment
sections.body:
Size: Large in the body, but reckon it by the arms — those take hold of you well before the beast itself arrives.
Durability: Hard to finish, and it mends. Arms you hew off grow back within a few weeks.
Defenses: Soft-bodied, but seldom seen: it shifts colour to whatever it lies against, squeezes into gaps no armed man could follow, and can blind the water with a cloud of ink whenever the fight turns.
Speed: It crawls slowly and swims moderately, but it can jet backward at startling speed in a straight line to break clear.
Might: Eight arms that seize and crush at once, and a beak beneath them to open whatever the arms have held still.
Mind: Cunning for a beast — territorial, patient, and quick to abandon a fight it is losing.
Disposition: Fiercely aggressive within its own ground and indifferent beyond it. It takes swimmers from below and drags them down.
Bane: The arms can be cut, and it feels the loss. Take enough of them and it quits the field entirely. Its ink only defeats a man who is relying on his eyes.

sections.title: How it fights
sections.body: It waits, coloured like the rock, then reaches with several arms at once, fastens, and crushes while the beak goes to work. Whatever it holds it drags away from air. When the fight sours it fills the water with black ink and jets backward out of it — it will not stay to die, and it will be waiting on the same ledge next season.

sections.title: Margin notes
sections.body:
• The arms reach you before the body does. Judge every distance by the arms.
• Cut arms, not body. Take enough of them and it withdraws of its own accord.
• When the ink comes, do not chase it blind. Back to a rock, and wait the cloud out.

sections.title: Parley (never)
sections.body: A beast, and no more — though a clever one. I watched a giant octopus work the lid off a lobster-creel with the patience of a locksmith, and thought for a moment somebody was home. Nobody was. It wants its ledge and whatever swims past it, and has no use for your words.

sections.body: Grave — A grave peril

sections.title: Special abilities
sections.body:
Severing Tentacles: An opponent can attack a giant octopus's tentacles with a sunder attempt as if they were weapons. Each tentacle can absorb 10 points of damage before it is severed. If a giant octopus is currently grappling a target with the tentacle that is being attacked, it usually uses another limb to make its attack of opportunity against the opponent making the sunder attempt. Severing one of a giant octopus's tentacles deals 5 points of damage to the creature. A giant octopus usually withdraws from combat if it loses four tentacles. The creature regrows severed limbs in 1d10+10 days.

Constrict (Ex): A giant octopus deals 2d8+6 points of damage with a successful grapple check.

Improved Grab (Ex): To use this ability, a giant octopus must hit an opponent of any size with a tentacle attack. It can then attempt to start a grapple as a free action without provoking an attack of opportunity. If it wins the grapple check, it establishes a hold and can constrict.

Ink Cloud (Ex): A giant octopus can emit a cloud of jet-black ink 20 feet high by 20 feet wide by 20 feet long once per minute as a free action. The cloud provides total concealment, which the octopus normally uses to escape a losing fight. All vision within the cloud is obscured.

Jet (Ex): A giant octopus can jet backward once per round as a full-round action, at a speed of 200 feet. It must move in a straight line, but does not provoke attacks of opportunity while jetting.

Skills: A giant octopus can change colors, giving it a +4 racial bonus on Hide checks. A giant octopus also can squeeze and contort its body, giving it a +10 racial bonus on Escape Artist checks. A giant octopus has a +8 racial bonus on any Swim check to perform some special action or avoid a hazard. It can always choose to take 10 on a Swim check, even if distracted or endangered. It can use the run action while swimming, provided it swims in a straight line.

lore.summary: A voracious thing of the temperate deeps, its body alone longer than a longboat and its ten tentacles reaching further than any spar you could set against them. It attacks very nearly anything it meets — whales, boats, men — and it is at home in water no daylight has ever reached.

sections.title: Hunter's assessment
sections.body:
Size: Huge in the body, and the tentacles make it far larger still. Nothing standing on a small deck is out of its reach.
Durability: Deeply tough and stubbornly hard to put down. It fights on well past the point where anything sensible would have sunk.
Defenses: No armour at all, but it lives where you cannot follow, hides behind a cloud of its own ink, and is fast enough to leave the moment it chooses.
Speed: Swift in the water, and swifter still when it jets away in a straight line. Out of the sea it has no life whatever.
Might: Ten tentacles that seize and crush together, and a beak that shears through whatever they hold up to it.
Mind: Dull and endlessly hungry. It attacks almost everything it comes across, without weighing the odds at all.
Disposition: Voracious and solitary. It holds no territory and defends nothing — it only feeds.
Bane: It cannot leave the water, and it cannot fight what stays beyond the tentacles. Hew those off one at a time; when enough are gone it breaks away and sinks out of the fight.

sections.title: How it fights
sections.body: It rises out of the dark, throws several tentacles over the rail or around the swimmer, and crushes while it draws the catch back to the beak. It grapples everything within reach at once and would far rather pull you under than kill you outright, since drowning costs it nothing. Beaten, it inks the water and jets away into deep water.

sections.title: Margin notes
sections.body:
• Axes at the rail, not swords. You are cutting rope-thick meat, not fencing with it.
• Never lash yourself to the boat in squid water. Men have gone over with the rail still attached to them.
• Where cachalots hunt, squid are stirred out of the deeps. Their quarrel is not with you, but your hull is in the middle of it.

sections.title: Parley (never)
sections.body: None whatever. It is a mouth with arms attached. I have seen a squid take a man off the sternpost while two of us had a hold of his belt, and it did not hurry over any part of it. Cut, and keep cutting. There is nothing else on offer.

lore.summary: Carnivorous fish of the cold seas, from lean grey things no longer than a man, through the middling sort that will kill you, to the true monsters — great whites longer than a fishing skiff. All of them will attack whatever comes near, provoked or not, and all of them smell blood in the water from further off than any lookout can see. The sahuagin keep them as a man keeps hounds.

sections.title: Hunter's assessment
sections.body:
Size: From man-length and merely dangerous, up to the great whites, which are monsters outright and want no help from anything.
Durability: Tough throughout, and the largest are very tough indeed. A wound does not slow them and does not frighten them off.
Defenses: Nothing but hide and speed. What truly protects a shark is the water, and your inability to see it until it has chosen.
Speed: Very fast — faster than a man swims, faster than most of what it hunts, and it never has to surface for breath.
Might: Jaws and nothing else, and the jaws are enough. A great white takes a limb in a single closing.
Mind: Nothing. It is appetite with fins on it.
Disposition: Aggressive without cause or warning. It hunts alone, in schools, and in packs where the water is rich.
Bane: It is helpless out of the water and it cannot sense anything above the surface at all. A boat, a rock, a ledge — anywhere out of the sea — and the hunt simply ends.

sections.title: How it fights
sections.body: It circles at the edge of sight, taking your measure, and then comes straight in and bites. There is no more craft to it than that and none is wanted. Blood in the water fetches every other shark for a great distance, and a pack will take a swimmer apart between one breath and the next.

sections.title: Margin notes
sections.body:
• Bleed into the sea and you have rung the dinner bell for every shark for leagues.
• Do not thrash. Go upright, get your back to something solid, and watch it circle.
• Where sahuagin raid, the sharks come first. Sharks in numbers mean spears behind them.

sections.title: Parley (never)
sections.body: No. The sahuagin can speak with theirs after a fashion, which is the business of pointing a hound at a hare, not conversation. To a shark you are only a question of whether you will fit. I have never met one that asked anything else.

lore.summary: The sperm whale: the greatest hunter in the sea, a blunt-headed leviathan as long as a merchantman's hull, that dives into lightless water to fight giant squid and comes up scarred for it. Its gentle kin the baleen whales strain the warm seas for creatures too small to see; its lesser cousin the orca, of cold water, attacks near enough anything it finds.

sections.title: Hunter's assessment
sections.body:
Size: Gargantuan — the largest thing most sailors will ever watch move.
Durability: Immense. It carries the whole weight of the deep on every dive and thinks very little of a spear.
Defenses: No armour, only bulk and depth. It goes where nothing can follow and stays under far longer than any man could hold on.
Speed: Steady rather than swift at the surface, but tireless, and it can sound out of your reach whenever it pleases.
Might: A bite that takes a giant squid apart, and a tail slap that stoves in a boat along with the men sitting in it.
Mind: Dull-witted but watchful, and it keeps company — the cachalot goes solitary or in pods, and a pod is a great deal of whale.
Disposition: No hunter of men. It hunts squid in the deeps and troubles a ship only when the ship has troubled it first.
Bane: It hears the world rather than sees it, singing into the dark and reading the echo. Kill the sound — lay a silence on the water about it — and it is left with eyes no better than your own, in a sea it has never needed them for.

sections.title: How it fights
sections.body: It fights as it hunts squid: it sounds, comes up from beneath, and closes its jaws. Against a boat it uses the tail instead, which is worse. It does not usually begin a quarrel, but it has the bulk to end one, and there is no manoeuvre a rowed boat can make that a whale cannot answer by simply being where it wishes.

sections.title: Margin notes
sections.body:
• It hunts by sound. If you must fight, foul the water with noise; better, be quiet and be gone.
• The tail is what kills boats, not the jaws. Never sit in its lee when it goes to sound.
• Hide scarred all over with sucker rings means the deeps are its ground and not yours. Do not follow it down.

sections.title: Parley (never)
sections.body: No words — but of every beast in this book, the cachalot is one I would rather leave alone. It has no quarrel with men. I have rowed within an oar's length of one lying up to breathe and been ignored entirely, and that is the whole of the parley, and quite enough of it.

Blindsight (Ex): Whales can "see" by emitting high-frequency sounds, inaudible to most other creatures, that allow them to locate objects and creatures within 120 feet. A silence spell negates this and forces the whale to rely on its vision, which is approximately as good as a human's.

It can use the run action while swimming, provided it swims in a straight line. *A whale has a +4 racial bonus on Spot and Listen checks. These bonuses are lost if its blindsight is negated.

Whale Kin: Cachalots, also known as sperm whales, can be up to 60 feet long and prey on giant squids. Two relatives share the entry. The baleen whale is a plankton-feeder between 30 and 60 feet long, such as gray, humpback, and right whales: Gargantuan Animal, Challenge Rating 6, Init +1, Speed swim 40 ft.; AC 16 (–4 size, +1 Dex, +9 natural), touch 7, flat-footed 15; Base Attack/Grapple +9/+33; tail slap +17 melee (1d8+18); Space/Reach 20 ft./15 ft.; Fort +14, Ref +9, Will +5; Str 35, Dex 13, Con 22, Int 2, Wis 12, Cha 6; warm aquatic; solitary. These massive creatures are surprisingly gentle, and if harassed or provoked they are as likely to flee as to retaliate. lore.summary: The great grey herds of the warm plains: herbivores that want nothing at all from you, and will still kill you for standing in the wrong place. Unpredictable is the honest word. The same stock gives the smaller, steadier beast of the east, which takes to training far better and carries men to war, and the shaggy mammoths and mastodons of colder ground.

sections.title: Hunter's assessment
sections.body:
Size: Huge — a moving wall, with its tusks set at about the height of your throat.
Durability: Prodigious. It carries wounds that would drop anything smaller and comes on regardless.
Defenses: Thick tough hide and nothing else, but the hide is a great deal. Arrows lodge in it and are ignored.
Speed: Faster over open plain than a running man, and it does not need to turn as sharply as you are hoping.
Might: Terrible. It gores with the tusks, slams with the trunk, stamps with the forefeet, and if you go down it walks over you without noticing.
Mind: Dull-witted but very attentive: its ears are its best sense and its nose is not far behind. The eastern strains take training well enough to be ridden into battle.
Disposition: Unpredictable, which is the whole of the danger. It will ignore you all morning and charge you at noon for no cause you could name afterward.
Bane: It charges in a straight line. Put something solid between you and step aside as it commits — a charging elephant cannot correct, and a herd in flight goes where its heads are pointed and nowhere else.

sections.title: How it fights
sections.body: It charges whatever it takes for a threat. The tusks come first and are the worst of it; then the trunk slamming and the forefeet stamping at whatever is still upright. A beast that size walking through your line tramples men flat without breaking stride, and a herd doing the same is not a fight at all, only a thing to be out of the way of.

sections.title: Margin notes
sections.body:
• Do not stand your ground. Tree or rock between you, and step aside as it commits.
• Downwind, always. It hears better than it sees and smells better than either.
• Between a cow and her calf is the shortest road to death on the plains. Walk the long way round the herd.

sections.title: Parley (never)
sections.body: None to be had, but restraint serves better here than any weapon. The elephant is not hunting you. Give the herd the road, keep downwind, keep your voices low, and nine times in ten they pass by without a glance. It is the tenth that gets written home about.

sections.title: Special abilities
sections.body:
Trample (Ex): As a full-round action, an elephant can move up to twice its speed and literally run over any opponents at least one size category smaller than itself. It merely has to move over the opponents in its path; any creature whose space is completely covered by the elephant's space is subject to the trample attack. If a target's space is larger than 5 feet, it is only considered trampled if the elephant moves over all the squares it occupies. A trampled opponent takes 2d8+15 points of damage, or half that with a successful Reflex save (DC 25). A trampled opponent can instead forgo the save to make an attack of opportunity at a –4 penalty against the elephant. The elephant merely has to move over the opponents in its path, and it can only deal trampling damage to each opponent once per round. The save DC is Strength-based.

Scent (Ex): An elephant can detect approaching enemies, sniff out hidden foes, and track by sense of smell, noticing other creatures within 30 feet by scent (60 feet if upwind, 15 feet if downwind) and detecting strong scents at twice those ranges.

Combat: Elephants tend to charge at threatening creatures. Massive herbivores of tropical lands, they are unpredictable but are nevertheless sometimes used as mounts or beasts of burden.

Indian Elephants and Prehistoric Kin: This entry describes an African elephant. Indian elephants are slightly smaller and weaker (Strength 28), but more readily trained (Wisdom 15). These statistics can also represent prehistoric creatures such as mammoths and mastodons.
